docs.title: Urban Solar Carver
docs.text:
GPU-accelerated generation of maximum developable building volumes that protect solar and daylight access in urban environments.

USC works by subtraction: it starts from a theoretical maximum volume, casts rays from the protected surfaces toward the sky, and removes the voxels that obstruct solar or daylight access beyond a configurable threshold.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• 6 carving modes covering solar access, passive heating, daylighting, and radiative cooling
  • 3-stage pipeline (preprocessing, thresholding, exporting); each stage can be re-run on its own
  • GPU-accelerated ray tracing via NVIDIA Warp (DDA kernel), with CPU fallback
  • Grasshopper plugin (27 components) for Rhino 3D integration
  • Python API, CLI, and Jupyter notebooks

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
Input (PLY meshes, EPW weather, YAML config)
    |
    v
Preprocessing ── scores.npy, voxel_grid.npy
    |
    v
Thresholding ─── mask.npy (binary carving mask)
    |
    v
Exporting ────── export.ply (or .obj/.stl/.glb, set by final_mesh_format)

Each stage reads the previous stage's manifest, so you can re-run thresholding with different parameters without re-computing scores.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:

  • Grasshopper Plugin: Rhino 3D integration, component list, daemon setup

docs.title: Criteria: chained carvings
docs.text:
A designer often protects different things with different criteria: the daylight of the neighbours' windows, the winter sun on a school yard, the PV potential of roofs. Each has its own test surfaces, its own sky or sun model and its own threshold. A chain carves them one after the other on one voxel grid, from a single config file.

Where this works today

Chains run from the CLI (usc run), the Python API (run_chain) and the daemon. The local service behind the browser app stores and runs projects with several criteria (see In the browser app's service), and Grasshopper chains two criteria through the after input of USC_ThresholdStage (see In Grasshopper). The browser app shows a project's criteria in the Criteria step, each with a switch, a menu and a panel (see Several criteria).

docs.title: What a chain is
docs.text:
A chain is an ordered list of criteria. Each criterion is one carving pass with its own mode, test surfaces, mode settings and carving rule (carve_fraction, threshold, smoothing, carve_above, max_slope_deg).

  • The maximum volume stays as drawn. Every criterion traces its rays over the same voxel grid, built once from the maximum volume, context and terrain. No mesh is made between criteria, so nothing is voxelized twice.
  • Each criterion decides among what the one before it kept. Its carve amount refers to the voxels still there when it starts: carve_fraction: 0.8 in the second criterion removes 80 % of the score over the voxels the first one kept, not 80 % of the whole volume. Its histogram, carve_above and slope limit act on those voxels too, and it never brings back a voxel an earlier criterion removed. The order therefore matters.
  • Exporting and massing build once, from the last criterion. Massing measures its floor plates against the maximum volume as drawn and its saved footprint, so the facades follow the drawn outline instead of the voxel staircase of the envelope.

A voxel's score is the weight of the rays that cross it, and it does not depend on which other voxels remain. So a criterion's scores are the same as in a run of its settings alone on the drawn maximum volume. Only thresholding depends on the criterion before it.

docs.title: The config file
docs.text:
Settings shared by the whole chain are at the top level, and the criteria are listed under criteria::

# Shared by the whole chain
max_volume_path: "site/maxVolume.ply"
context_path: "site/surroundings.ply"
epw_path: "weather/athens.epw"
voxel_size: 1.0
out_dir: "outputs"

criteria:
  - id: daylight
    name: Daylight on neighbours' windows
    mode: daylight
    test_surface_path: "protect/windows.ply"
    carve_fraction: 0.7
  - id: winter-sun
    name: Winter sun on the yard
    mode: benefit
    test_surface_path: "protect/yard.ply"
    start_month: 11
    start_day: 1
    start_hour: 8
    end_month: 2
    end_day: 28
    end_hour: 16
    carve_fraction: 0.8

Relative paths are resolved against the folder of the YAML file, as in any config. A file with a criteria: list is a chain file, and load_config refuses it: use load_chain, or let usc run choose.

docs.title: Shared settings and criterion settings
docs.text:
Belongs to Settings Each criterion id, name, mode, test_surface_path; the carving rule (threshold, carve_fraction, score_smoothing, carve_above, carve_above_min_consecutive, max_slope_deg); the mode's own settings (the analysis period start_month .. end_hour or an analysis_period: mapping, sun_steps_per_hour, min_altitude, time_basis, balance_temperature, balance_offset, simulated_weights_path, include_harm, tilted_plane_angle_deg, dew_point_celsius, bliss_k, min_sky_elevation_deg); rays_per_patch and edge_taper Shared by the chain max_volume_path, context_path, terrain_path, context_blocks_rays, voxel_size, grid_step, ray_length, device, epw_path, out_dir, north_deg, margin_frac, and the exporting and massing settings (min_voxels, apply_smoothing, final_mesh_format, ground_floor_height, floor_height, min_plate_dimension, plate_tolerance, plate_stacking, diagnostics, diagnostic_plots)

In code the first row is urbansolarcarver.chain_config.CRITERION_KEYS; every other config key is shared. Putting a shared setting inside a criterion, or a criterion setting at the top level, is an error that names the setting, so a file never means two things. -o overrides on the command line set shared settings only.

epw_path is shared but only reaches the criteria whose mode reads a weather file (time-based, irradiance, benefit). A daylight criterion in the same chain does not receive it, so it raises no warning about an unused setting.

Ids. A criterion's id names its output folder, so it is 1 to 40 letters, digits, _ or -, and ids are unique ignoring case (Windows and macOS ignore case in folder names). The names Windows reserves for devices (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1 to COM9, LPT1 to LPT9) cannot be folder names there and are refused. Without an id the criterion gets its position (1, 2, ...). Without a name the display name is its mode.

Every criterion is validated when the file is loaded. An error in a criterion's settings starts with criterion <id> (<name>):; an error in an id or in where a setting is placed names the criterion's position.

The preprocessing manifests do not record a chain root. Each criterion voxelizes the same maximum volume, and thresholding checks the grid (voxel size, origin, shape and occupancy) of the previous criterion instead.

docs.title: Running a chain
docs.text:
usc validate -c chain.yaml          # lists the criteria and the shared settings
usc run -c chain.yaml               # criteria in order, then exporting
usc run -c chain.yaml --produce massing

usc run runs preprocessing and thresholding of each criterion in order, then exporting (or massing) from the last. --start-from thresholding reuses every criterion's existing scores and thresholds the chain again.

From Python:

from urbansolarcarver import run_chain

result = run_chain("chain.yaml", out_dir="outputs", produce=("exporting", "massing"))
result.criteria[0].thresholding.retention_pct   # what the first criterion kept
result.exporting.export_path

run_chain(chain, out_dir=None, produce=("exporting",), start_from="preprocessing", context=None, trace=None, threshold_from=None) accepts a path or a ChainConfig from load_chain, and returns a ChainResult: one PipelineResult per criterion, then exporting and massing (None when not produced) and the issues of the call. An issue of a criterion's stage is named criterion <id> (<stage>).

With start_from="preprocessing", trace is a collection of criterion ids: only those criteria trace their rays again, and the others keep their existing preprocessing folder (StageChainError when it is missing). Thresholding runs for every criterion from the first one that traced on, so a criterion decides after the existing run of the one before it. threshold_from names a criterion, earlier in the chain than the first traced one, whose thresholding is run again as well. With start_from="thresholding", every criterion is thresholded again, or, with threshold_from, only that criterion and the ones after it; the ones before it keep their thresholding folders (StageChainError when one is missing). A trace that names no criterion of the chain (an empty one too, with start_from="preprocessing") and a threshold_from that is not in the chain (with either start) raise ValueError before anything is touched. The default of both is the behaviour without them: every criterion traces and thresholds.

The daemon runs a chain when a run request names a chain file; its overrides set shared settings only, and its trace_criteria and threshold_from_criterion keys are these two arguments (see Engine requests).

docs.title: Output folders
docs.text:
outputs/
  criteria/
    daylight/
      preprocessing/   scores.npy, voxel_grid.npy, footprint.json, manifest.json, diagnostics/
      thresholding/    mask.npy, manifest.json, diagnostics/
    winter-sun/
      preprocessing/
      thresholding/
    chain.json         the criteria in order, with the thresholding run of each
  exporting/
  massing/             (when produced)
  run_report.md

The run report has a "Criteria" section with one row per criterion (name, mode, rule, cutoff with its unit, voxels at start, voxels kept). With two or more criteria a "Chain" section follows: the maximum volume (the filled voxels the first criterion started with), the volume left after each criterion in m³ and its share of the maximum volume, and the total time covers every criterion's analysis and carving. Its Configuration, Preprocessing and Thresholding sections describe the last criterion.

docs.title: One step of a chain
docs.text:
thresholding takes the previous criterion's result as an optional input, after:

usc thresholding -c winter_sun.yaml --from outputs/criteria/winter-sun/preprocessing/manifest.json \
    --after outputs/criteria/daylight/thresholding --out outputs/criteria/winter-sun/thresholding

This step needs a single-criterion config (winter_sun.yaml holds the settings of one criterion): usc thresholding reads it with load_config, which refuses a chain file. Give --out the criterion's own folder as above; without it the result goes to <out_dir of the config>/thresholding, and a later usc run -c chain.yaml --start-from exporting would build from the criterion that is in the chain's folder. The output folder may not be the previous criterion's own (StageChainError).

from urbansolarcarver import thresholding

thr2 = thresholding(pre2, cfg2, "outputs/criteria/winter-sun/thresholding", after=thr1)

--after and after take the folder or the manifest.json of the previous criterion's thresholding (the Python function also takes its result). The mask of this run is never True where the previous mask is False.

  • The manifest records after_manifest and after_run_id, and the diagnostics record voxels_at_start, the voxels this criterion decided about.
  • Both criteria must share the grid (maximum volume, context, terrain, voxel size and margin). Otherwise a StageChainError names the voxel size, origin, shape or a different maximum volume. A difference in the context or the terrain shows up as a different maximum volume.
  • When the previous criterion re-runs later, the criteria after it are refused with StageChainError until they are thresholded again, as for any stage.
  • When the previous criterion kept no voxel, the mask is empty and the run reports the issue nothing_left_to_carve.

docs.title: Changing a criterion is cheap
docs.text: Scores do not depend on the other criteria, so an earlier criterion's settings change only the thresholding of the criteria after it, which takes seconds. Only a change to a criterion's own mode settings or test surfaces, or to a shared setting such as the voxel size, needs its rays traced again. To change the carve amount of the first criterion and see the effect on the whole chain, edit it and run usc run -c chain.yaml --start-from thresholding.

docs.title: In the browser app's service
docs.text:
The local service behind usc ui keeps the criteria of a project in project.json and writes the project's config.yaml as a chain file from them, so a project folder also runs with usc run -c <folder>/config.yaml. Each criterion has its own test surface files: a file is stored once in the project, several criteria can use it, and the engine reads one joined file per criterion. A criterion's id is a number the service assigns (1, 2, ...); it names the criterion's output folder and stays the same when the criteria are reordered.

A run does only what changed. The service compares each criterion's settings and test surfaces with the ones its results were made from, and asks the engine to trace only the criteria whose rays changed (trace_criteria), then to threshold the chain from the first traced criterion on. When a criterion earlier in the chain needs thresholding again while a later one is traced, it also sends threshold_from_criterion; when no criterion needs tracing, it thresholds the chain from the first criterion whose thresholding is out of date on (threshold_from_criterion), so the ones before it keep their results. The result of each criterion, the volume each one kept and the criterion that removed each voxel are served per criterion.

On the packaged Perimeter block example (Solar time-based, then Daylight on the same test surfaces; NVIDIA RTX 3060), the first analysis took 2.4 s and kept 187,743 m³. After adding the Daylight criterion, the next analysis traced only that criterion and took 2.7 s; the chain then kept 187,743 m³ after the first criterion and 119,848 m³ after the second. The app shows a row for each criterion, runs only the ones that changed and shows the carved voxels by criterion in 3D (see Several criteria). Projects made with an earlier version open as a chain of one criterion with their results still current. The routes, the files and the rules for what goes out of date are in Criteria in a project.

docs.title: In Grasshopper
docs.text:
USC_ThresholdStage has an after input, the last one: the thr_result of the thresholding stage of the criterion before. Empty, it behaves as before. To chain two criteria, give the second one its own Config (a different out_dir), Preprocess and ThresholdStage, and connect the first ThresholdStage's thr_result to the second one's after. The second stage decides only among the voxels the first one kept and never keeps one it removed. USC_Export and USC_Massing connected to the second criterion's Config and results then build from what both criteria kept. See Grasshopper.

The daemon request behind it is a run that starts at thresholding with the after key (RunRequest.after; run_pipeline(..., after=...) in Python). A request with after and a chain file, or with after and a start_from other than thresholding, gets a ConfigError reply: a chain file links its criteria itself, and a stage that does not run thresholding would ignore after without a message. An engine older than this feature would ignore the key and run the second criterion on its own, so the ping reply lists the engine's features, and usc_gh.run_stages pings first when after is given. For an engine without run_after it raises "The UrbanSolarCarver engine running now is older than this definition and cannot chain criteria. Restart it from USC_Session." and sends no run request.

docs.title: Grasshopper Plugin (Rhino 3D)
docs.text: USC provides 27 custom Grasshopper components for visual parametric workflows in Rhino.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Copy all .ghuser files from grasshopper/USC_GHplugin/ to your Grasshopper User Objects folder, or drag them onto the Grasshopper canvas. Requires Rhino 8 (the components are Python 3 script components).

docs.title: Updating components on existing canvases
docs.text:
Components already placed on a canvas keep the code they were placed with. After installing new .ghuser files, drop USC_SyncCanvas (ribbon: Session) on the canvas:

  1. Leave update unconnected and read report: it lists which USC components are up to date and which would change. Components whose code you edited by hand count as outdated and would be overwritten.
  2. Connect a Button to update and click it. Components whose inputs and outputs are unchanged are replaced in place, keeping position, wires, internalised values (Set One String), graft/flatten/simplify settings, enabled/preview state and group membership. Components whose inputs or outputs changed are placed beside the old one inside a red group that names the new or removed ports: rewire the new component, then delete the old one and the group.
  3. The whole update is one undo step (Ctrl+Z). If anything fails mid-update, the canvas is rolled back and the error appears in report.

By default the updates come from the installed user objects (Grasshopper's User Objects folders); wire a folder path into folder to update from elsewhere, e.g. grasshopper/USC_GHplugin in a checkout.

docs.title: Rebuilding the components
docs.text:
The .ghuser files are generated from the sources in grasshopper/components/; edit the .py, never the .ghuser. Each source declares its own ports: names and descriptions in its "GH UI" block, order and types in the numpydoc Inputs / Outputs docstring. grasshopper/components.json holds the ribbon subcategory and the stable user-object GUID; icons are grasshopper/icons/<source name>.png (24x24).

Code shared by several components (daemon calls, the run command wrapper run_stages, engine issues shown as warnings by show_issues, loading the engine's mode_registry.py and archetype_defaults.py by path with engine_module, PLY reading and writing, mesh conversion, override parsing) lives in grasshopper/usc_gh.py. The components load it at run time from <carver_root>/grasshopper/, where carver_root is the repository folder given to USC_Session, so editing it takes effect on the next solve without rebuilding any .ghuser. It uses only the standard library, RhinoCommon and the Grasshopper SDK, because the component scripts run in Rhino's own Python, not in the USC environment.

pip install -e .[ghbuild]                       # pythonnet
python grasshopper/build_ghuser.py              # rebuild into USC_GHplugin/
python grasshopper/build_ghuser.py --check      # exit 1 if any .ghuser is stale

The builder uses GH_IO.dll from the Rhino 8 install (--ghio <folder> to point elsewhere); Rhino does not need to be running. Rebuilds are byte-for-byte reproducible, so an unchanged source leaves its .ghuser untouched. tests/test_gh_components.py checks that every source's UI block matches its docstring and that every docstring type maps to a Grasshopper type hint.

A component already placed on a saved canvas keeps the code it was placed with; USC_SyncCanvas updates it (see above).

docs.title: Smoke test in Rhino
docs.text:
tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py solves examples/USC_components_for_grasshopper.gh in a running Rhino 8 (through RhinoCode.exe) and compares two runs, for example main against a branch. It needs Rhino open, so it is not part of pytest. Run it with the USC environment's python:

python tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py run main D:\path\to\urbanSolarCarver
python tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py run branch D:\path\to\worktree
python tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py compare main branch

run stops any running daemon, fills the template definition in memory (root panel, output folders, EPW, start_daemon and run toggles, pipeline 1's geometry from examples/test_inputs/multiple_buildings), solves it with the root's usc_gh.py and daemon, stops the daemon again and closes the definition without saving. A root without .venv, venv or python_path.txt (a worktree) gets a python_path.txt pointing at the python running the script. The report (messages and output counts of every USC component) and the output folders go to ~/.urbansolarcarver/gh_runs/<label>, a short path because deep output folders exceed Windows' 260-character limit. Each run keeps its output there (about 120 MB for the example), replaced by the next run with the same label; delete the folder when done. The definition's start_daemon toggle also switches on verbose, so the daemon opens its own console window during a run. With several Rhinos open, pass --rhino <ID> from RhinoCode.exe list.

compare matches components by nickname and occurrence, compares their messages (paths, ids and timings removed) and output counts, the meshes byte for byte, integer and boolean arrays (masks) exactly and float arrays (scores) to a relative difference of 1e-5, since GPU atomic adds sum in a varying order (about 1e-7 between runs). It exits with 1 when anything differs.

docs.title: Daemon
docs.text:
The components send their work to a persistent daemon process that keeps the CUDA context and compiled kernels loaded, so repeated runs skip the start-up cost:

urbansolarcarver daemon start       # start GPU daemon
# ... use Grasshopper components ...
urbansolarcarver daemon stop        # stop when done

The daemon binds to localhost only. Clients authenticate with a random key that the daemon generates on first start and stores in ~/.urbansolarcarver/.daemon_authkey.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The ribbon shows each component as USC <Name> (for example USC Session). Below they are listed by their source file name in grasshopper/components/, grouped by ribbon tab.

Session (0::Session)

  • USC_Session: finds the USC Python environment and starts or checks the daemon. Wire a Boolean True to start_daemon to launch the daemon; when the input is unconnected or False, the component only reports whether a daemon is running.
  • USC_SyncCanvas: updates the USC components on the canvas to the installed versions (see Updating components on existing canvases)

Configuration (1::Config)

  • USC_Config: builds a pipeline configuration from a mode, an EPW path, an output folder, an optional base YAML and the override strings of the parameter components below. With no YAML, the daemon starts from the mode's starting values (for example the analysis period of the benefit, irradiance and time-based modes) and applies the overrides; configs/ is not read. Spellings such as time_based or tilted-plane are accepted.
  • USC_Mode: selects the carving mode by number and outputs its name for USC_Config's mode input. The mode list and descriptions come from the engine (mode_registry.py), so solve USC_Session first; without it the component shows a message that says so.
  • USC_EPW (USC EPW Path): passes the EPW file path
  • USC_AnalysisPeriod: defines the analysis date/time range
  • USC_GridSettings: voxel size, surface sampling spacing (grid_step), grid padding (margin_frac)
  • USC_RaySettings: ray length, minimum sun altitude, north direction (north_deg), context_blocks_rays (Account for context blocking: with context or terrain, whether the rays that hit them are dropped; default true), and rays_per_patch (rays per sky patch in the weighted modes: 1, 4, 9 or 16; default 4)
  • USC_BenefitParams: benefit-mode hour weighting: balance temperature and offset (simple weights), or a simulated_weights.json artifact plus the experimental include_harm toggle (simulated weights)
  • USC_TiltedPlane: fixed-angle envelope parameters
  • USC_RadCooling (USC Radiative Cooling): radiative cooling parameters (dew point, Bliss constant)
  • USC_Threshold: thresholding strategy, score smoothing, column carve-above post-processing, and the slope limit (max_slope; empty = 75 degrees for the weighted modes, 90 = off). Connect its output to USC_ThresholdStage's threshold_overrides input (not Config) so threshold changes only re-run thresholding.
  • USC_Postprocess: smoothing and cleanup settings. Connect its output to USC_Export's postprocess_overrides input (not Config) so mesh cleanup changes only re-run export.
  • USC_Diagnostics: detailed score statistics and diagnostic plot images

Pipeline execution (2::Main)

  • USC_RunPipeline: runs all three stages in one go (quick prototyping)
  • USC_Preprocess: runs preprocessing only (ray tracing + scoring). Errors turn the component red.

Both take the geometry: max_volume, test_surfaces, and the optional context (existing buildings and large trees that stay) and terrain (the ground), each a list of Meshes or Breps. Context removes every voxel column of the max volume it overlaps and, with context_blocks_rays on, drops the rays that hit it; terrain removes only the voxels below the ground and drops the rays that hit it. See Context and terrain. Leave them unconnected for a run without them.

  • USC_ThresholdStage: runs thresholding only. Accepts threshold_overrides directly. Its summary shows the slope limit (angle, voxels removed, share of the obstruction score). Errors turn the component red.

To chain two criteria, give the second one its own Config (a different out_dir), Preprocess and ThresholdStage, and wire the first ThresholdStage's thr_result into the second one's after input (the last input; empty = a single criterion as before). The second stage then decides only among the voxels the first kept and never keeps one it removed. A daemon started before the update cannot chain; the component then says so and asks for a restart from USC_Session. - USC_Export: runs exporting only. Accepts postprocess_overrides directly. Errors turn the component red. - USC_Massing: stage 4, builds floor plates from the carving mask (inputs config, thr_result, massing_overrides, run; outputs closed Breps, floor areas per floor and in total, and the plates.json path). See Floor-plate massing. - USC_MassingSettings: floor heights, module size, tolerance and stacking for USC_Massing. Connect its output to USC_Massing's massing_overrides input so changes re-run only massing.

The stage components send the daemon's run command, each producing its own stage, and read the stage folders from the reply. A stage reads the output of the stage before it from <out_dir>/<stage> of its Config, so Preprocess and the stages after it need the same Config out_dir; the pre_result and thr_result inputs order the solve and still have to be connected. Conditions the engine reports (a setting the mode ignores, nothing carved, a footprint that could not be read, ...) appear as warnings on the component, one per issue, as <stage>: <message>. Re-running preprocessing makes the stages after it refuse their old output until they run again (the error names the stage to re-run).

Simulated weights (3::Weights)

  • USC_Archetype: assembles a typical building for the simulated weights from the five parameter families below; every input is optional (neutral defaults, read from the engine's archetype_defaults.py, so solve USC_Session first)
  • USC_ZoneGeometry / USC_ZoneFabric / USC_ZoneVent / USC_ZoneOperation / USC_ZoneShading: Honeybee-style family feeders for USC_Archetype: shoebox dimensions + per-facade window-to-wall ratio, envelope U-values + g-value + mass class, air-change rates + heat recovery, setpoints + internal gains, and declared shading coefficients. Each family is one wire into USC_Archetype.
  • USC_SimulateWeights: runs the ISO 13790 5R1C simulation through the daemon; outputs the simulated_weights.json path (wire into USC_BenefitParams) and a heatmap preview image

docs.title: Input geometry
docs.text:
Context should be closed bodies (Breps or closed Meshes): the voxels it takes are found by an inside test, and an open context gives a context_not_closed warning. Terrain may be an open sheet. A test surface on the face of a context building (a neighbour's facade) is not blocked by that face; one drawn inside a context mass or under the terrain has all its rays blocked and gives a test_points_blocked warning.

Test surfaces must be individual flat panels. If you are using extruded block boundaries or any joined polysurface, explode it into its faces before connecting it to USC_Preprocess. Otherwise the planarity check rejects the combined surface and preprocessing fails with a "No points sampled" error.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
Use the decomposed pipeline (Preprocess → ThresholdStage → Export as separate components) rather than RunPipeline. This lets you:

  • Adjust threshold parameters (USC_Threshold → USC_ThresholdStage) and re-export without re-running the expensive ray-tracing step.
  • Adjust mesh cleanup settings (USC_PostProcess → USC_Export) and regenerate the mesh without re-thresholding or re-preprocessing.

Only USC_Preprocess needs to re-run when you change geometry, mode, or the analysis period.

docs.title: Inspect
docs.text:
A test surface is read from one side only. A carving and a Simulate study see the side its normal points to: a surface that faces into a building, or a roof that faces down, sees nothing, so the criterion barely protects it and nothing else in the app says so. Inspect shows which way every test surface faces, lets you turn the ones that face the wrong way by clicking them, and gives a short summary of every input mesh file.

Inspect is a workspace beside the pipeline, like Simulate. It runs no engine step, changes no criterion or setting and makes nothing out of date by itself. Only Save and Restore original change a file, and only when you press them.

USC does not decide which way a surface should face. Only you know whether a surface is a roof for PV, a facade, or a soffit that faces down on purpose. Inspect shows the orientation and leaves the choice to you.

docs.title: Design, Simulate and Inspect
docs.text:
The switch Design | Simulate | Inspect in the header, next to the project name, changes the workspace. Inspect hides the steps and gives the 3D view the whole window. Switching away keeps Design's step and scroll position and Simulate's selection as they were. The Layers menu and the viewer tools are the same in all three; Inspect adds one layer, Surface orientation.

Inspect works while a run of the project is going. Only Save and Restore original wait for it to end, as uploads do.

docs.title: The Files panel
docs.text:
The Files panel floats over the top left of the 3D view and collapses to an icon. It lists the input mesh files by role: maximum volume, test surfaces, existing surroundings and terrain. The weather file has no geometry and is not listed. Each row gives the file name, its triangle count and its area. A file that cannot be read stays in the list with its problem, for example a broken export, and has nothing to select.

Pressing a row selects the file. The view frames it and draws the other test surface files faint, so you see what the selected one faces. The selected row also opens the file's summary:

  • Bounds: the minimum and maximum corner in the file's own coordinates. When a corner is more than 10 km from zero, a note says the coordinates look georeferenced and how far they are. Under the list, the panel says which point the view is drawn around, since the view uses a local origin.
  • Surfaces, for a test surface file: how many surfaces it has (below).

An earlier version also counted closed bodies. It was dropped: CAD exports (Rhino's OBJ, for one) keep a corner per face, with that face's normal, so faces share no edges and every face counted as an open body (Allatini's maximum volume: 0 of 24). The voxelizer does not depend on it either: it fills by ray crossings along three axes with a two-of-three vote, so a missing floor or a T-junction does not change the voxels.

The summary is worked out when Inspect asks for it, not at upload, and it is kept until the file changes. The test surface and maximum volume files are read as the engine's loader reads them, with their normals made consistent, so the triangles you see are the ones the engine uses. The surroundings and terrain files are read as stored, without that step, as the engine reads them too: nothing reads their orientation, and fixing it takes seconds on a large mesh.

docs.title: What the colours and face normals mean
docs.text:
Test surfaces are drawn two-sided. The side the normal points to has the test surface colour of the viewport theme. The back side is orange. A surface that is the wrong way round therefore shows orange when you look at it from outside, whichever side of it the camera is on.

The Face normals box in the panel draws one normal per surface, an arrow from its centre along its normal, 0.3 times the square root of its area long, between 1 m and 10 m. One per surface rather than per triangle keeps a large file readable. The normals do not take clicks. A surface you have turned and not saved is drawn, and its normal points, the new way.

The maximum volume is drawn see-through, and the surroundings and the terrain grey, as in Design. Their orientation is not drawn: nothing reads the orientation of the surroundings and terrain, and the loader turns the closed bodies of the maximum volume outward by itself.

docs.title: Surfaces, and why a click turns a whole surface
docs.text:
A surface is a set of triangles joined by shared edges, as the engine's loader reads the file. A click in flip mode turns the whole surface under the pointer, not the single triangle. The loader makes neighbouring triangles agree in winding, so a lone triangle turned in the file would be turned back the next time the file is loaded.

For the same reason a test surface file that is closed as a whole cannot be flipped. The loader turns every closed body outward, so its surfaces would come back the way they were. Such a file shows This file is closed as a whole, so its surfaces cannot be flipped. and its Flip mode and Flip all buttons are off.

docs.title: Flipping
docs.text:
Flipping applies to test surface files only. Select a test surface file, then:

  • Flip mode (a toggle on the selected row): a click on a surface turns it, and a second click turns it back.
  • Flip all turns every surface of the file, for a whole export that came out the wrong way round.

Turns are staged. The view shows them at once and the row says, for example, "3 surfaces turned, not saved". Nothing is written until you press Save, so the criteria go out of date once, not at every click. Discard drops the staged turns.

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
Save writes the file once, in its own format:

Format What is written OBJ The coordinates with 10 decimals PLY float64 coordinates GLB, STL float32, as these formats hold nothing finer; coordinates are kept as precisely as the format allows

A GLB or STL that another program wrote with coordinates float32 cannot hold exactly may have a corner move by about one float32 step when it is saved: for a GLB that is about 4 µm at 50 m from the file's whole-metre offset, for an STL about 0.25 mm at 4 km from zero. OBJ and PLY corners do not move.

The service then reads the written file back with the engine's loader and compares it with what you turned. If the triangles or their normals are not what was written, or a corner moved by more than 1 µm (for GLB and STL, more than two float32 steps at the file's largest coordinate), nothing is saved and the file stays as it was. A saved file keeps the geometry only. USC reads geometry only, so OBJ groups, materials and texture coordinates and PLY colours are not in the saved file. The original, which is kept (below), still has them.

Save has the effects of uploading the file again through the app:

  • The joined files of the criteria and studies that list the file are built again.
  • Those criteria and studies go out of date, and the criteria after them have to carve again. A run traces the file again.
  • The file's record in project.json is renewed. There is no "changed in the project folder" notice, since you made the change in the app.

Save and Restore original are not available while a run of the project is going. The panel says so beside the buttons.

docs.title: A file that changed in the project folder
docs.text:
Turns are staged on the version of the file Inspect read, and Save sends that version with them. Before it writes anything, the service builds the files changed in the project folder into the project, as when the window comes back to the front, and compares the file stored now with that version. If you replaced the file by hand meanwhile, even with one that has as many triangles and surfaces and the same bounds, Save writes nothing and says The file changed in the project folder since its surfaces were turned, so nothing was saved. Its staged turns are dropped, since the surfaces of the new version are numbered anew, and Inspect reads the files again. Restore original does the same with The file changed in the project folder since Inspect read it, so nothing was restored., so it never puts an older original over a file you replaced. The kept original of a file replaced by hand is dropped (below), and the file has a "changed in the project folder" notice as any file replaced by hand.

Inspect also reads the files again when the stage status finds a file changed in the project folder, for example when the window comes back to the front, so turns staged on a replaced file are dropped before you press Save.

docs.title: Restore original
docs.text:
Before the first save of a file, the file as it was is kept in the project folder, in inputs/originals/test_surfaces/. Restore original puts it back byte for byte, with the same effects as a save, and removes the kept copy. The button shows on the selected row while an original is kept.

The kept original is dropped when you upload a file with the same name, when you remove the file in the app, and when you replace the file by hand in the project folder. After that the stored file is the only version, and Restore original is not offered.

docs.title: Leaving Inspect with turns not saved
docs.text:
Switching to Design or Simulate while a file has staged turns, or while a save or restore is under way, asks Save the turned surfaces before leaving Inspect? with three answers: Save (writes every file with turns, then leaves), Discard (drops them and leaves) and Stay. While a save is under way the dialog says A save is under way.; Save and Discard wait for it, and when it is written with nothing left to save the dialog leaves by itself. If a save is refused, the one under way included, for example because a run is going or the file changed in the project folder, the dialog stays open with the reason, so a failed save is never left unseen in another workspace.

If a file changed while turns were staged on it (a new version uploaded, or replaced in the project folder), the staged turns are dropped and the panel says The file changed, so its turns not saved were dropped. The surfaces of the new version are numbered anew, so the old turns would not mean the same surfaces.

docs.title: Where the service keeps things
docs.text:
The service computes all of this in local_web_service/inspection.py, with trimesh, from the stored files as the engine's loader returns them, so the view and a flip use the triangles the engine uses. No engine function is involved. Routes (all under /api):

Route What it does GET /projects/{name}/inspect The summary of every mesh file of the project; allowed while a run is going GET /projects/{name}/inspect/test_surfaces/{file}/geometry The triangles of a test surface file with a surface number per triangle, as one binary (layout in inspection.inspection_geometry) POST /projects/{name}/inspect/test_surfaces/{file}/turn Turn the surfaces named in surfaces of the file of version and save the file; 409 while a run of the project is active, or with stored_file_changed: true when the file stored now is not that version; 422 for a file closed as a whole, one that cannot be read, a surface that does not exist, or a file changed in the folder that cannot be read; 500 when the written file does not read as turned POST /projects/{name}/inspect/test_surfaces/{file}/restore Put the kept original back in place of the file of version; 404 when none is kept, 409 while a run is active or (stored_file_changed) when the file stored now is another

Each file of the summary has a version, the sha256 of its bytes. A turn or a restore names it, and both first build the files changed in the project folder into the project. The service keeps the summary of each file it read, and for a test surface file its triangles and their surfaces, up to 32 files and 5 million kept triangles, the least recently used leaving first.

docs.title: Not in Inspect
docs.text: Inspect does not change axes (Y-up), coordinates in the millions, open volumes or heavy files, and it does not flag surfaces that probably face the wrong way. It does not inspect the envelope, the massing or the joined files. Further checks (a Y-up guess, the estimated voxel grid before a run) are planned separately.

docs.title: Floor-plate massing
docs.text: The massing stage turns the carved envelope into stacked floor plates: a ground floor, then floors of equal height, each a closed prism whose outline follows the maximum volume's footprint and steps back where the envelope does not allow the floor. Use it for massing models, floor-area figures and as simulation input (one closed prism per floor and plate).

docs.title: How plates are formed
docs.text:
1. Footprint and facades. The footprint is the maximum volume's plan projection (the area it covers seen from above), so an uneven or raised base does not change it. Preprocessing saves this footprint (footprint.json in its folder, world coordinates) from the mesh it voxelized; massing reads that file, not the mesh in the config passed to massing and not the mesh file on disk, so later edits to either change nothing. If preprocessing could not compute a footprint, massing uses the outline of the occupied voxel columns and warns. The footprint outline is split into facades wherever it turns by more than 30 degrees. Curved or faceted outlines with smaller turns stay one facade. A facade whose vertices all lie within 1 cm of the line from its first to its last vertex is straight: footprints cut from meshes carry vertices micrometres off a straight wall. Far from the origin, where a mesh stored in float32 rounds its coordinates by more, the tolerance is four of those float32 steps, and it is never more than half a voxel. A real bend, a few degrees over a few metres, stays a bend.
  2. Faces. Every footprint column belongs to its nearest facade. Facades shorter than two modules (2 * min_plate_dimension: chamfers, small steps) get no face of their own; their neighbours meet at one corner across them. At corners the longer facade takes the corner square (up to half the building's depth behind it), so every face ends in a line perpendicular to its facade. At equal lengths (a square) the facade closer to the x axis takes the corner. Along a facade not aligned with the voxel grid, the voxelizer also fills columns whose centre lies just outside the footprint; such a column belongs to the face of the footprint point nearest to it, so the end of a slab is cut on the same lines as the rest of it.
  3. Bays. Each face is cut into square modules of min_plate_dimension (3 m): along its facade, perpendicular to it, and in depth behind it, parallel to it. Along a straight facade the rows of modules are laid from both ends of the building (its extent along the facade) towards the middle; what is left over widens the middle row, or the two middle rows equally (a 10 m bar: 3, 4 and 3 m; 13 m: 3, 3.5, 3.5 and 3 m). An end wing therefore starts with a whole row whatever the building's length, and the cuts on the two sides of a straight building line up. Along a curved facade the rows are cut every module of length from its start. A row narrower than a module at the end of a face that ends inside the building (at a corner square) joins its neighbour, and a module at the back of a row (where the face meets the one opposite) shallower than min_plate_dimension joins the one in front of it. Each module is built on its own, so a wing keeps its floors whatever the envelope does behind it in the same face, for example a courtyard of a perimeter block carved lower. Behind any facade a plate can therefore be as shallow as one module, min_plate_dimension.
  4. Floors. For each floor (ground floor ground_floor_height, then floor_height), a module is built when it stays inside the maximum volume over the floor's full height, at most plate_tolerance of its volume lies outside the carved envelope, and (with plate_stacking: supported) it is built on the floor below. A column along a facade not aligned with the voxel grid counts only for its share inside the footprint, so whether a module is built does not depend on the angle of the footprint to the grid; a column less than half inside the footprint need not be filled by the maximum volume at all (along a wall the voxels can reach up to a voxel past the footprint, as the re-voxelized envelope of an earlier carving does). A module over the tolerance is not built even when built modules enclose it, so a local dip in the envelope can leave a hole of one or two modules in a floor; holes are not filled. Parts narrower than min_plate_dimension are dropped (the test is the same at any angle of the footprint to the voxel grid), so a strip one module deep, min_plate_dimension, is kept. The ground floor starts at the maximum volume's lowest point, and the top floor ends at or below its highest point; preprocessing records both in its manifest. The voxel grid is not aligned with these points, so the lowest occupied voxel layer can lie mostly below the base (its centre below it) and the highest mostly above the roof. Such a layer is filled only where rays hit the base or the roof, which they miss in columns along facades that are not aligned with the grid, so it does not count: a floor's height and its share outside the envelope are measured over the layers whose centre lies between the lowest and the highest point. A preprocessing run from before the manifest recorded these points starts the ground floor at the bottom of the lowest occupied layer and lets the top floor reach the top of the highest occupied layer, up to one voxel outside the maximum volume at each end; running preprocessing again gives the floors above.
  5. Plates. The connected built modules of a floor form a plate. A module on a straight facade is drawn as a rectangle in its facade's frame: cuts lie on the cut lines (along the facade and in depth), the back of the last module lies on the midline where the facade faces a parallel one, and the facade edges are the footprint's own. Other edges (face ends at corners) are within half a voxel of the voxel columns. Where a corner is not square, the faces of its two facades meet along the bisector of the corner; a module there is its rectangle cut by that line (or by a line of the two facades' corner squares, or by a bisector with a facade that meets one of them; where the faces meet along a curve, by the line midway between the two faces' columns turned to a direction of the two facades or their bisector), so it ends on one straight slanted edge. A cut that would leave an angle under 30 degrees or a piece narrower than a voxel is not used. Modules on curved facades, and the modules no such line separates from a neighbouring face, follow their voxel columns, straight to within half a voxel; they stay off the columns of modules not in the plate. Where the shapes of two modules overlap, the overlap belongs to one of them, so plates of different modules never overlap. Spikes and cracks of no width that the boolean operations leave are removed.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning ground_floor_height 5.0 Height of the ground floor (m) floor_height 3.0 Height of every floor above it (m) min_plate_dimension 3.0 Side of the square module and minimum plate width (m); "Grid module" in the browser UI plate_tolerance 0.2 Largest share of a module's volume on a floor outside the carved envelope; "Permitted volume exceedance" in the browser UI plate_stacking supported supported: build a module only on a built module; free: each floor on its own

Plates never leave the maximum volume. The three sizes must be at least the voxel size of the preprocessing run; the stage reports an error naming the setting otherwise.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In <out_dir>/massing/:

  • plates.json: one entry per plate (floor, z bottom and top, outline and holes in world coordinates, area, number of modules (bays), share of its volume outside the envelope), plus the floor area per floor and in total;
  • plates.obj: one closed mesh per plate, named floor_<n>_plate_<m>, written whatever final_mesh_format says (the browser interface draws it and reads its parts by name);
  • plates.ply, plates.stl or plates.glb when final_mesh_format is one of them: the same plates, as one mesh in PLY and STL (formats without named parts) and with one named part per plate in GLB. The manifest names this file as export_mesh_path (plates.obj itself for OBJ). A change of final_mesh_format reruns massing as well as exporting. Far from the origin (georeferenced models) PLY keeps the coordinates in double precision and GLB places the offset in each node, while STL can only hold float32 and the run reports a float32_coordinates issue when that rounds them by more than 1 mm;
  • manifest.json and diagnostics/diagnostic.json (floors built, plates, floor areas, share of the carved envelope inside plates, volume placed outside the envelope through the tolerance, footprint source).

The run report gets a Massing section.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
• Python: massing(thr_result, cfg, out_dir)
  • CLI: usc massing -c config.yaml (finds the thresholding manifest of the run, or pass -f)
  • Grasshopper: USC_Massing after USC_ThresholdStage, with USC_MassingSettings

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Floors count from the lowest point of the maximum volume; a part that starts higher gets a warning (sloped ground is not supported yet).
  • If the maximum volume's footprint cannot be read from the mesh, or does not match the voxel grid (more than 5% of the occupied voxel columns more than one voxel outside it, for example when the file was replaced after preprocessing), the voxel footprint is used, with a warning; plates can then be up to one voxel larger than the true footprint.
  • Modules are rectangles in their face's frame; there are no interior zones (core, perimeter) and roofs are flat.

docs.title: Carving Modes
docs.text: USC supports six carving modes, each using a different strategy to determine which voxels to remove from the maximum buildable volume.

docs.title: Mode overview
docs.text: Mode Type Weight Source Requirements time-based Violation count Sun vectors from EPW EPW + analysis period irradiance Weighted Perez all-weather sky EPW + analysis period benefit Weighted Heating-benefit sky EPW + analysis period (+ balance temperature or a simulated-weights file) daylight Weighted CIE overcast luminance None (no EPW, no analysis period) tilted_plane Binary Geometric fixed angle Angle specification only radiative_cooling Weighted Martin-Berdahl + Bliss Dew point temperature (no EPW)

docs.title: Sky patches and rays per patch (rays_per_patch)
docs.text:
The four weighted modes divide the sky into the 145 Tregenza patches, give each patch a weight, and trace rays from every test point toward the patches its surface faces. A voxel's score is the weight of the rays that cross it.

With rays_per_patch: 1 each point sends one ray to each patch centre. The centres are 12° apart in altitude (12° to 60° in azimuth), so the rays of one point reach a voxel layer at distance d about 0.21 × d apart. Rays from the other points of a test surface fill the space between them only up to the surface's own extent. Beyond about five times the height of the test surfaces, voxels between the rows of rays get no ray at all and score 0, and the scores show horizontal and diagonal bands. On the Allatini example (facades 8 to 24 m high, maximum volumes 30 to 190 m away), 38 % of the maximum volume's voxels scored 0 and the tallest tower column scored 0 over four bands 4 to 12 m high.

rays_per_patch 4 (the default), 9 or 16 trace that many rays per patch. The patch is cut into 2 × 2, 3 × 3 or 4 × 4 cells of equal solid angle, and each ray points at a place in its cell drawn from a hash of the test point, the patch and the cell, carrying that share of the patch weight. Neighbouring points draw different places, so their rays no longer line up into rows. The places depend on nothing else, so a run gives the same scores every time and for any batch size; CPU and GPU agree to float32 rounding (their sine and cosine can differ in the last bit, so a ray grazing a voxel edge may cross the neighbour). Rays that the surface does not face are skipped, so a patch its plane cuts counts the part in front of it: a wall sees exactly half of the overcast sky.

Measured in daylight mode on an RTX 3060. Allatini (19,193 test points), against 64 rays per patch; District of many buildings (527,000 test points, test surfaces beside the volumes, so little banding at 1 ray):

rays_per_patch Allatini: voxels scoring 0 Allatini: keep or carve decisions at 70 % that differ Allatini: preprocessing District: preprocessing 1 38 % 30 % 1.15 s 12.3 s 4 6 % 6.4 % 1.18 s 13.9 s 9 5.5 % 4.7 % 1.20 s 15.2 s 16 5 % 3.8 % 1.33 s 17.0 s

The remaining zeros are voxels that no test point sees (behind context, or behind the surfaces). The sub-rays are generated inside the tracing kernels, so memory does not grow with them. The rays are ordered by patch, so the GPU threads that run together trace the same direction from neighbouring points and find the voxels they visit in its cache; this is what keeps the extra rays cheap. rays_per_patch: 1 reproduces the scores of earlier versions. Time-based mode traces sun positions and tilted_plane its planes, so neither reads this setting.

docs.title: Context and terrain
docs.text:
Two optional meshes describe what is around (or inside) the site and stays whatever is built: context_path for existing buildings and large trees, terrain_path for the ground. Both are opaque. Balconies, external shading devices and billboards are not context. Without them a run is the same as before.

Context does two things, in every mode:

  • Whole columns go. Where the context lies in a voxel column of the maximum volume (a voxel of the grid counts when its centre lies inside the context, not on its surface), the whole column is removed from the buildable mass, above and below the context. Nothing is built on top of kept buildings, under tree crowns or beside a chimney within its columns. To build on or over an existing building, remove it from the context. A context face shared with the maximum volume (a party wall) takes no voxel of the site. Only the context bodies that reach the voxel grid count here, so a large city model around the site costs little and its distant parts cannot disturb the result.
  • Rays that hit it are dropped (ray-based modes: time-based, irradiance, benefit, daylight, radiative_cooling). Each ray from a test point is tested against the context mesh before scoring; a ray that hits it within ray_length adds nothing to any voxel, because that sun or sky is lost whatever is carved. The test is against the mesh, not the voxel grid, so context far outside the grid still blocks. Weights are not renormalised: a test point whose sky is half hidden keeps half its weight in play.

Terrain blocks rays exactly like context, but removes only the voxels whose centre lies below the ground (where the terrain crosses the column's vertical centre line, the highest crossing if there are several). The rest of the column stays buildable, so a sloping site keeps its volume above the ground. A voxel centre on the ground counts as above it. An open sheet is fine; a column the terrain does not cover keeps all its voxels.

Test surfaces on context buildings. A neighbour's facade is usually a face of its own context building. Each ray starts 1 cm off the test surface along its normal and hits closer than 1 mm are ignored, so a test surface lying on a context face is not blocked by that face; other parts of the same building (a second wing) block normally. A test surface drawn inside a context mass, below the terrain, or facing into its own building has all its rays blocked: the run reports a test_points_blocked warning with their count (ray-based modes), since those points protect nothing.

tilted_plane traces no rays to the sky, so context and terrain only remove voxels there: the planes are the same as without them.

Account for context blocking (context_blocks_rays, on by default). Off, the context and the terrain still remove their voxels and still count as solid mass, but no ray is tested against them: the carving is the one that ignores what they block, on the same reduced maximum volume, for comparison. The run report says when it is off. Dropping the rays lowers the scores, so with it on the cutoff usually needs another look.

Context and ground are solid. The rule that keeps a facade's own building from counting as its obstruction (a voxel the facade plane passes through, with mass behind it, is the facade's own skin) treats everything inside the context and below the terrain as solid mass, like the maximum volume. The space under a tree crown or above a kept building is not solid: a column removed there is empty, and a sliver of the maximum volume left in front of it counts as an obstruction like any thin part of the maximum volume.

Context mesh not closed. The column rule needs closed (watertight) context bodies to tell inside from outside. An open context mesh gives a context_not_closed warning: where an open body reaches the voxel grid, the columns removed may be too few or too many. It still blocks rays.

The run report (and summary["context"] in the preprocessing diagnostics) gives the voxels removed by the context columns and below the ground, the volume and share of the maximum volume removed, the rays dropped and their share of the ray weight, and the test points with every ray blocked. Everything after preprocessing (thresholding, carve_above, the slope limit, export, massing) sees the reduced maximum volume; the massing footprint leaves out the columns context took.

docs.title: Thresholding strategies
docs.text: USC supports three threshold strategies. The right choice depends on the mode.

docs.title: For weighted modes (irradiance, benefit, daylight, radiative_cooling)
docs.text:
Scores are continuous weighted sums: the sky-patch weight of every ray a voxel blocks, times the area of protected surface that ray's sample point stands for (about grid_step² m², times its edge_taper weight when that is set). The score is then a physical quantity that does not change with the sample spacing:

Mode Score unit A voxel's score is irradiance kWh the solar energy (direct and diffuse) it keeps from the protected surfaces over the analysis period benefit kWh the same for the heating-useful solar energy only (the hours below the balance point, or the simulated weights) daylight m² the overcast sky it hides from the protected surfaces, weighted by CIE overcast brightness, in m² of fully hidden sky radiative_cooling m² the night sky's cooling potential it hides, in m² of fully hidden sky

The patch weights of irradiance and benefit are kWh/m² per patch (Ladybug's sky matrix), counted on a surface facing the patch: there is no reduction for the angle at which a ray meets its surface, so the kWh are those a surface turned towards each sky patch would receive. The daylight and radiative_cooling weights are each patch's share of its sky and sum to 1, so 1 m² is the whole sky of 1 m² of open horizontal surface (a vertical facade sees half of it at most). Summed over a set of voxels a score counts what they block more than once when a ray crosses several of them; it compares voxels, it is not an energy balance. Scores written before this unit was introduced (preprocessing manifests without score_unit) were sums of patch weights without the area, and changed four times when the sample spacing halved.

Strategy How it works When to use carve_fraction (default) Removes the highest-scoring voxels until the removed part holds the target fraction of the building's total obstruction weight, counting the voxels that carve_above removes with them. 0.7 = aggressive (tall, slim volumes). 0.3 = conservative (bulky volumes). Recommended. Works as a slider; no knowledge of the score distribution needed. headtail Jiang (2013) head/tail breaks: splits the scores at their mean, then splits the part above the mean again, for as long as that part holds at most 40% of the values. Suited to heavy-tailed distributions. When you want an automatic, data-driven split without choosing a fraction. Numeric value Manual cutoff on the scores, in the score unit above. Voxels scoring above this value are carved. Advanced. Pick it from the score histogram in diagnostics/ (or the browser UI's). It means the same at any sample spacing, but depends on the weather, the period and the protected surfaces, so it carries over between variants of one project rather than between projects.

How carve_fraction and carve_above work together. With carve_above (the default), a column loses everything above its lowest removed voxel. Each voxel therefore goes at the cutoff of the lowest high-scoring voxel below it, and carve_fraction counts the score of everything removed that way: 0.4 removes 40% of the obstruction score. (Before this was counted, carve_above removed extra score on top of the value set, so 0.4 removed 50-62% in the ReSBE test blocks.)

Slope limit (max_slope_deg, default 75 degrees for these modes). Scores in a column are low near the ground, peak partway up and fall again, and a column is cut at its lowest voxel above the cutoff. Two neighbouring columns whose peaks fall just above and just below the cutoff end 10-15 m apart, and small score differences leave single-column spires. After carve_above, each column may rise at most tan(max_slope_deg) above a 5 x 5 median of its neighbours' heights; anything higher is removed. Cliffs become ramps and spires end one step above their surroundings. The limit only removes voxels, and carving more before it never keeps more after it. In the ReSBE test blocks (33 m, 0.5 m voxels) it cut the spike area from 26-186 m² to 0-25 m² for 0-10% of extra obstruction score, reported as obstruction_fraction_carved_by_slope_limit (it is not counted in carve_fraction). The median window and the allowed step are counted in voxels, so at 1 m voxels the limit is weaker than at 0.5 m. 90 turns it off. Finer sampling (grid_step) reduces spikes only a little; they come from the column rule, not from rays missing voxels.

All three strategies, the score smoothing and the reported retention consider occupied voxels only. Rays also cross the empty cells of streets, courtyards and the grid margin, and those cells typically hold 60-80% of the total score mass; including them would make the result depend on how much air the grid contains.

docs.title: For violation-count modes (time-based, tilted_plane)
docs.text:
time-based scores measure how much protected surface a voxel shades, and for how long, in m²·h: the shaded test-surface area times the duration, summed over the analysis period. Each sample point stands for about grid_step² m² of surface and each sun position for 1/sun_steps_per_hour h, so the score does not depend on the sampling density.

Threshold value Meaning 0 (default) Strict: remove any voxel that shades any protected surface at any sampled moment 5 Tolerate a voxel that shades up to 5 m²·h, e.g. 5 m² of facade for one hour, or 1 m² for five hours None Uses the default (0 = strict)

String strategies (carve_fraction, headtail) do not apply to violation counts and raise an error. tilted_plane is strictly binary (see below).

Physically interpretable thresholds

The time-based threshold has a direct meaning: threshold: 0 means zero shadow tolerance during the analysis period; threshold: 5 lets each voxel cast up to 5 m²·h of shadow on the protected surfaces. A numeric threshold of a weighted mode is read the same way in its unit: threshold: 20 in irradiance keeps a voxel that blocks up to 20 kWh over the period.

docs.title: time-based
docs.text:
Casts rays from test surfaces along actual sun vectors for specific dates and times. Each voxel's score is the shading it causes (m²·h, see above); with the default threshold: 0, a voxel is carved if any sun ray passes through it. There is no sky-patch weighting.

The sun is sampled sun_steps_per_hour times per hour (default 12, i.e. every 5 minutes). The sun moves about 15° of azimuth per hour, so hourly sampling leaves gaps between the ray sheets of consecutive hours in which mass survives while still shading the protected surface between samples; at 1 m voxels, 5-minute sampling closes them for obstructions up to ~40 m away. Ray count grows linearly with this value.

docs.title: Time basis: standard, daylight saving or solar time (time_basis)
docs.text:
By default (time_basis: standard) the hours of the analysis period are the EPW's local standard time.

With time_basis: daylight_saving they are daylight saving (summer) time: standard time plus one hour, on every date of the period, so 13:00 is read as 12:00 standard time. Weather files carry no daylight saving dates (TMY files leave the EPW header's field empty), so USC does not look up when the clocks change: a period that runs past the change of the clocks is one hour off on the days outside summer time. Split such a period, or use standard time.

With time_basis: solar they are true solar time: 12:00 is the moment the sun crosses the meridian, due south at a northern mid-latitude site, on every date. Solar-fence rules (Boulder: 21 December, two hours each side of solar noon) and the Japanese shadow regulation define their hours this way.

The two clocks differ by the equation of time (between about −14 and +16 minutes over the year) plus the site's distance from its time-zone meridian (4 minutes per degree of longitude). Solar noon in standard time:

Site 11 Feb 21 Jun 3 Nov 21 Dec Golden, CO (bundled EPW, 105.2° W, UTC−7) 12:15 12:03 11:44 11:59 Athens (23.7° E, UTC+2) 12:39 12:27 12:09 12:23

So a 10:00-14:00 window read in standard time is up to 39 minutes off a 10:00-14:00 solar-time rule in Athens, and the carved envelope shifts with it. Ladybug computes the sun position in either clock (is_solar_time).

time_basis is read by time-based only. daylight_saving and solar are refused in irradiance and benefit: their analysis period selects hourly EPW records, which are in standard time, so reading the period in another clock would pair each hour with the wrong weather record. Modes without an analysis period (daylight, tilted_plane, radiative_cooling) ignore it with the usual "does not use" warning. In the browser UI it is Time (Standard time / Daylight saving time / Solar time) under "More sun settings"; in Grasshopper it is the time_basis text input of USC Analysis Period.

mode: time-based
analysis_period: {st_month: 12, st_day: 21, st_hour: 10, end_month: 12, end_day: 21, end_hour: 14}
time_basis: solar   # 10:00-14:00 true solar time

Use case: protect direct sunlight during specific hours (e.g., winter solstice 10:00-14:00).

Threshold semantics: see violation-count thresholds above.

docs.title: irradiance
docs.text:
Weights each Tregenza sky patch by its cumulative direct + diffuse irradiance over the analysis period, using the Perez all-weather sky model. Voxels blocking high-irradiance patches receive higher scores.

Use case: climate-based solar resource assessment over an entire heating or cooling season.

docs.title: benefit
docs.text:
Similar to irradiance, but weights hours by a heating-benefit criterion. Two weightings are available:

Simple weights (default): only hours when the outdoor temperature is below balance_temperature - balance_offset contribute to patch weights. This protects solar access in the hours when it is useful for passive heating.

Use case: maximize passive solar heating potential during the heating season.

Key parameters: balance_temperature (free-running balance point; default 15 °C, typically about 12 °C for commercial to 18 °C for residential buildings), balance_offset (dead-band width, default 2 °C).

Cold period: urbansolarcarver.cold_period.cold_period_from_weather_file(epw_path, base_temperature) gives the start and end dates of the site's cold period, to use as the analysis period: the longest run of days whose 31-day running mean dry-bulb temperature (wrapping across the new year) is below the base, for benefit mode balance_temperature - balance_offset. It may wrap across the new year. Hours the EPW marks missing (99.9) are left out. The browser UI offers it as a preset of the analysis period. With simulated_weights_path set, the balance values are unused by the mode, so the cold period found from them describes the simple rule, not the simulated building. In climates whose temperature stays near the base all year, the longest run can be short and its dates arbitrary.

docs.title: Simulated weights
docs.text:
Instead of the binary cold-hour rule, benefit mode can consume hourly weights derived from a thermal simulation of a typical building (the compact 5R1C hourly model from ISO 13790). For every hour of the year the simulation answers: if one extra watt of sun arrived in this hour, how much less heating, and how much more cooling, would the building need over the whole year? This captures thermal lag (a noon gain stored in the mass and released into the cold evening still earns credit), diurnal mass state, and gain saturation, none of which the binary rule can express. The simple rule is the special case where the weights are 0 or 1.

Generate the weights once from an EPW and a building archetype (roughly ten numbers describing a typical building; the easiest form is a shoebox with per-facade window-to-wall ratios, see configs/archetype_example.yaml):

urbansolarcarver simulate-weights -e weather.epw -a configs/archetype_example.yaml

This writes simulated_weights.json (the weights plus full provenance) and a .png preview of the weights next to it. Then point a benefit config at the artifact:

mode: benefit
simulated_weights_path: simulated_weights.json
# include_harm: true   # experimental: also subtract summer-overheating contributions

A full-year analysis_period is the natural choice with simulated weights, since the schedule itself selects the useful hours. balance_temperature / balance_offset are unused (USC warns if you customize them). With diagnostic_plots: true, the run's diagnostics include a comparison dome showing how the simulated weights shifted the sky relative to the simple rule.

Use case: benefit envelopes that respond to the thermal mass, insulation, and glazing of the building stock being protected.

Key parameters: simulated_weights_path, include_harm (experimental; without declared seasonal shading (shading_hot in the archetype) harm is overstated, so treat it as a bracketing scenario).

See Simulated Benefit Weights for the engine's documentation (what it implements, how it was validated against RC_BuildingSimulator, the archetype inputs, and the declared limitations) and Tutorial 5 (examples/5_benefit_5r1c.ipynb) for an end-to-end walkthrough.

docs.title: daylight
docs.text:
Weights sky patches using the CIE standard overcast sky luminance distribution. Direct sun is not considered: each patch's weight is its overcast-sky luminance, which depends on the zenith angle, times its solid angle, scaled so the weights sum to 1. No weather file or analysis period is needed.

Use case: protect diffuse daylight access (e.g., for daylighting codes, visual comfort).

docs.title: tilted_plane
docs.text:
Traditional geometric solar envelope method. Every voxel above a tilted plane at a fixed angle from each test surface is carved. No weather data is involved. Each sample point casts one ray at the plane angle, outward along the facade's horizontal normal, and every voxel at or above that ray in its (x, y) column is removed: the whole half-space above the plane, not only the band the rays cross. Where two test-surface panels meet at a convex corner or kink, their rays diverge; extra rays from the corner sweep the headings between the two normals, so the plane rotates around the corner (at 45 degrees, a column outside a right-angle corner is capped at its distance from the corner). Concave corners need no extra rays: the two planes already meet there.

The angle can be a single float (applied uniformly) or a list of 8 floats (one per compass octant N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW, chosen by the direction each facade faces).

Use case: quick regulatory envelopes, traditional Knowles-style solar access planes.

Key parameter: tilted_plane_angle_deg

Threshold semantics: this mode is strictly binary: a voxel either protrudes above the cut plane or it does not. Do not set threshold; leave it unset (the default None). Setting any string method or a numeric value > 0 raises a validation error.

docs.title: radiative_cooling (experimental)
docs.text:
Weights sky patches by their radiative cooling potential, using the Martin-Berdahl atmospheric emissivity model and a Bliss angular attenuation factor. The aim is to keep access to the cold sky dome for passive nighttime cooling. The model uses one representative night-time dew point and reads no weather file.

Use case: hot-arid climates where nighttime radiative cooling is a significant design strategy.

Key parameters: dew_point_celsius, bliss_k, min_sky_elevation_deg (optional: ignore sky patches below this elevation and renormalize the rest)

Warning

This mode is experimental. The clear-sky assumption may not hold in humid or cloudy climates.

Horizontal surface assumption

The current implementation assumes a horizontal analysis surface (flat roof). The angular view-factor weighting (cosθ/π) is only valid for upward-facing surfaces. Applying these weights to tilted or vertical test surfaces will over-weight the zenith and under-weight low-altitude sky patches, producing inaccurate cooling envelopes.
