docs.title: Pipeline orchestration
docs.text: File Purpose __init__.py Package entry point. load_config, build_config and user_config are imported directly; run_pipeline, PipelineResult, stages_to_rerun, the four stage functions and their result types are loaded from api.py on first access, so import urbansolarcarver and light CLI commands do not import torch or Warp. api.py Public facade. Defines run_pipeline(config, out_dir, produce, start_from, context, after), the sequencer (after is the previous criterion's thresholding, passed to the thresholding stage): it runs the stages needed for produce, each writing into <out_dir>/<stage>, and returns a PipelineResult (one Result per stage that ran, plus the run's issues). Also re-exports run_chain() and ChainResult (chained carvings, api_core/chain.py), stages_to_rerun(), preprocessing(), thresholding(), exporting(), massing(), their result types, load_config() and build_config(). api_core/__init__.py Collects the three stage modules and their result types into one importable sub-package. api_core/preprocessing.py Stage 1. Voxelizes the max-volume mesh into a dense 3D grid, samples test surfaces into evenly spaced points with outward normals, generates rays toward sky patches (or sun positions, or the tilted-plane direction, depending on mode), traces them through the grid with the DDA kernel, and writes the per-voxel obstruction scores to scores.npy. Also writes voxel_grid.npy, footprint.json (the plan projection of the voxelized mesh, which massing reads), the sample points and normals, the manifest, and diagnostics (JSON always; plots with diagnostic_plots: true). api_core/thresholding.py Stage 2. Loads scores.npy from Stage 1, optionally applies Gaussian score smoothing (weighted modes), applies the selected thresholding strategy (carve_fraction, headtail, or a numeric cutoff) to the raw scores of the occupied voxels together with carve_above (column_postprocessing.carve_above_scores, so carve_fraction counts what carve_above removes), applies the slope limit (column_postprocessing.limit_column_slope; 75 degrees by default for the weighted modes), and writes the binary mask mask.npy and scores_compared_with_cutoff.npy (the values the cutoff was applied to, which the browser UI draws its histogram from). Can be re-run with different threshold parameters without re-computing scores. With the optional after input (the previous criterion's thresholding result, folder or manifest) it decides only among the voxels that criterion kept: the manifest records after_manifest and after_run_id, the diagnostics voxels_at_start, and an empty start gives the issue nothing_left_to_carve. api_core/chain.py Chained carvings. run_chain(chain, out_dir, produce, start_from, context, trace, threshold_from) runs preprocessing and thresholding of each criterion of a chain in order into <out_dir>/criteria/<id>/<stage> (each thresholding gets the previous one as its after input), writes criteria/chain.json, then exporting and massing from the last criterion. trace limits the criteria that trace their rays again, and threshold_from starts thresholding at an earlier criterion than the first traced one, or, with start_from="thresholding", at that criterion instead of the first. Returns a ChainResult. See Criteria. api_core/massing.py Stage 4. Reads the thresholding chain, builds floor plates with floor_plates.py, writes plates.json (world outlines), plates.obj (one closed prism per plate), the manifest, diagnostics and the run report with a Massing section. floor_plates.py Floor-plate massing geometry: base outline and facades split at corners, faces by nearest facade with squared corners, faces cut into square modules (along the facade and in depth), floor-by-floor module selection (tolerance, maximum volume, stacking, minimum width), plate outlines and closed prisms. api_core/exporting.py Stage 3. Loads the binary mask from Stage 2, removes small disconnected voxel clusters, reconstructs a triangle mesh (cubic voxel faces, or SDF-smoothed marching cubes with Taubin polishing), writes export.<format>, and writes run_report.md for the whole run. api_core/_stage_io.py The start and end of a stage (begin_stage, commit_manifest), manifest paths relative to the manifest's folder (stored_path) and reading an upstream manifest with its run ID check (load_upstream). api_core/_util.py Helpers shared by the stages: config resolution, device resolution ("auto" → "cuda" or "cpu"), JSON writing, reloading the occupancy grid, config snapshots. api_core/_diagnostics.py Writes each stage's diagnostic.json and, with diagnostic_plots, its plots (write_preprocessing_diagnostics, write_thresholding_diagnostics) after the stage's compute; score histograms, sky-patch hemisphere plots, the simple-vs-simulated weight comparison dome, score statistics, NaN/Inf issues. matplotlib loads when a plot is drawn. api_core/_reporting.py run_report.md generation.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text: File Purpose surface_sampling.py Test-surface sampling. Discretizes each planar test-surface component into a regular grid of points with outward normals, projecting each face into its local 2D plane and using Shapely contains_xy for the in-polygon test; also computes the edge_taper weights and the analysis-mesh quads (AnalysisMesh). sample_surface is the preprocessing entry point. voxelization.py Converts a watertight mesh into a dense cubic boolean grid at the configured voxel_size, using the Warp parity voxelizer (voxelize_solid_warp, kernel in warp_kernels.py) (trimesh's rasterize-and-fill when Warp cannot run on the device) and filling enclosed cavities; the grid is cached in the active CarverSession. voxelize is the preprocessing entry point. context_geometry.py Context and terrain on the max volume's lattice. context_occupancy: voxels whose centre lies inside the context (parity voxelizer, centre rule only, rays spanning the context's bounds). remove_context_columns: the column rule. ground_heights / remove_below_ground: the voxels below the terrain. build_blocking_mesh / drop_blocked_rays: one Warp BVH of context and terrain, and the rays that hit it (dropped before scoring). drop_blocked_sky_sub_rays: the same per jittered sky sub-ray, as a skip mask. subtract_columns: the footprint without the removed columns, for massing. meshing.py Mesh reconstruction. Removes small disconnected voxel clusters with scipy.ndimage.label and converts carved voxel masks back to triangle meshes, either as cubic voxel faces or through signed-distance-field smoothing, marching cubes, and Taubin polishing. finalize_mesh is the exporting entry point. io.py Mesh file I/O. load_mesh: reads a mesh through Trimesh (PLY, OBJ, STL...), rejects files without triangles, and runs fix_normals on meshes that are not watertight. save_mesh: writes a mesh; PLY files switch to double-precision vertices when float32 would round the coordinates, GLB files (save_glb) carry a whole-metre offset in their nodes, and STL files, float32 only, report a float32_coordinates issue when that rounds them by more than 1 mm. validate_inputs checks that the files a preprocessing run needs exist; load_meshes loads the maximum volume and the test surfaces and reports coordinates a float32 PLY file has rounded.

docs.title: Carving engines
docs.text: File Purpose carving.py The three carving strategies. carve_with_sun_rays (time-based): traces rays from test-surface points toward the sun positions of the analysis period and returns the carved grid and per-voxel hit counts. carve_with_sky_patch_rays (irradiance, benefit, daylight, radiative_cooling): traces rays toward the 145 Tregenza sky patches (rays_per_patch per patch: the centre, or jittered sub-rays spread over the patch), weights each ray by its share of its patch's mode-specific value, and returns the accumulated per-voxel scores. carve_with_planes (tilted_plane): traces one ray per sample point at the plane angle (per-octant angles supported) and removes every voxel at or above it in its column. column_postprocessing.py The column rules thresholding applies after the score threshold: carve_above_columns() and carve_above_scores() (the carve_above setting) and limit_column_slope() (max_slope_deg), as numba kernels. ray_tracing.py Ray generation and voxel traversal. trace_and_score_dda / trace_and_count_dda: launch the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) kernels that step each ray through the voxel grid cell by cell and add the ray's weight (or a count of 1) to every voxel it crosses; they run on CUDA or on Warp's CPU backend, and there is no other tracer. follow_mass_behind_skin_dda: the skin rule. SkySubRays: passed to the wrappers, has the kernels trace each sky-patch ray as side² jittered sub-rays whose directions they compute themselves (no sub-ray arrays are stored); mesh_blocks_sky_sub_rays tests them against context and terrain, sky_sub_ray_directions returns them. generate_sky_patch_rays / generate_sun_rays: expand sample points × directions into flat ray arrays, keeping only directions the surface faces. auto_batch_size: picks a ray batch size from the free GPU memory. warp_kernels.py Warp setup and every Warp kernel of the package (DDA traversal, jittered sky sub-ray directions, skin rule, parity voxelizer, ground heights, mesh any-hit test), kept in one module so Warp compiles and caches them as one unit. dda_backend_available: whether the DDA backend can run on a device; require_dda_backend raises WarpBackendUnavailableError with the reason when it cannot. warmup_kernels: precompiles the kernels.

docs.title: Sky and sun models
docs.text: File Purpose sky_patches.py Tregenza hemisphere subdivision (145 patches) used by the weighted carving modes. fetch_tregenza_patch_directions: the 145 unit direction vectors. fetch_tregenza_patch_solid_angles: the solid angle (sr) of each patch. tregenza_patch_cells: each patch's band of altitude and share of azimuth. sub_ray_directions: the NumPy definition of the jittered sub-ray directions the kernels compute (a hash of point, patch and cell picks a place in each cell of equal solid angle); patch_facing_margin: how far behind a surface a patch centre can lie while the surface still faces part of the patch. compute_EPW_based_weights: for irradiance and benefit, builds a Ladybug SkyMatrix (Perez all-weather model) from the EPW's direct-normal and diffuse-horizontal irradiance over the analysis period, each computation in a temporary folder of its own; benefit keeps only the hours below the balance point, or scales each hour by simulated weights. For daylight, returns the CIE standard overcast luminance distribution (brightest at the zenith, no EPW). compute_radiative_cooling_weights: long-wave cooling potential per patch from the Martin-Berdahl clear-sky emissivity with Bliss angular attenuation, for a horizontal surface; patches near the zenith get higher weights than those near the horizon. sun.py Solar position vectors. get_sun_vectors: uses Ladybug's Sunpath with the location from the EPW header to return unit vectors toward the sun for each sampled date-time of the analysis period (sun_steps_per_hour per hour), dropping positions below min_altitude and rotating by north_deg; time_basis says whether the date-times are local standard time, daylight saving time (one hour ahead) or true solar time. sample_period builds the analysis date/time list with Ladybug's AnalysisPeriod. weather_file.py read_weather_file: parses an EPW file with Ladybug once per path, modification time and size, and returns a ParsedWeatherFile that hands out copies (the location, the hourly dry-bulb temperatures, a Wea of the solar irradiance), so one caller's change cannot reach another. Used by the sun vectors, sky weights, cold period, simulated weights and the service's sun path. scoring.py Sky-patch weight dispatch and threshold selection. get_weights: calls the weighting function for the selected mode (Perez irradiance, heating benefit, CIE daylight, or radiative cooling). carve_fraction_threshold: the score cutoff above which the voxels hold a given fraction of the total score mass (two-pass weighted histogram, O(N)). headtail_threshold: Jiang (2013) head/tail breaks for heavy-tailed score distributions. Inside a CarverSession, get_weights is cached, keyed by every argument and by the contents of the EPW and simulated-weights files. simulated_weights.py Simulated benefit weights (opt-in via simulated_weights_path). Implements the ISO 13790 Annex C hourly thermal model ("5R1C": five conductances, one lumped mass capacitance, one zone) in NumPy, and derives the hourly marginal benefit/harm of solar gain by perturbation: for each hour of the year, one watt of solar gain is added and removed and the change in annual heating and cooling demand is attributed to that hour (benefit[t] / harm[t], both in [0, 1]; all 17,521 year-simulations, the base run plus two per hour, march as one vectorized batch). generate_simulated_weights: EPW + archetype → simulated_weights.json artifact with provenance metadata plus a .png heatmap preview. ZoneParams.from_archetype builds the thermal network from about 10 physical inputs; expand_shoebox derives all areas from a width/length/height + per-facade window-to-wall ratio shorthand. Validated against ETH's RC_BuildingSimulator (tests/data/oracle_5r1c_reference.json). Design note: design/simulated-weights.md.

docs.title: Sun and sky check (Simulate)
docs.text: File Purpose check_settings.py The metrics of the check (CHECK_METRICS: sun hours, solar energy, useful solar gains (key useful_solar_energy), overcast sky component, cooling sky, sky view factor, each with its unit, whether it reads the weather file and which mode's starting period it takes), the metric each carving mode starts with (DEFAULT_CHECK_METRIC), CheckSettings (period, time basis, lowest sun altitude, rays per patch, sample spacing, ...) with for_config, settings_digest (sha256 of the settings without the weather file's path) and build_check_settings. Standard library and Pydantic only, so the service lists the metrics without importing torch. solar_check.py The check itself. check_directions: the sun positions of the period (one an hour), or Tregenza's 145 sky patches traced with the carving's jittered sub-rays, each with its value. evaluate_test_points: traces the directions of every test point against a closed mesh with Warp's BVH ray queries, an envelope or massing clipped by the maximum volume, the context and terrain blocking in every geometry. solar_check and simulate_study: sample the test points at the carving's spacing (at most MAX_CHECK_POINTS, 2 million), trace every geometry and write check_points.npz, check_values.npz and check_summary.json with the fingerprints of what the result came from. Behind the engine request check. check_files.py The files of the sun and sky check without torch: the result file names, file_fingerprint, and run_geometry_files (the envelope and massing a run folder has built, with the surface tolerance from their manifests), which solar_check.run_geometries and the service both use.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: File Purpose mode_registry.py One ModeSpec per carving mode, in Grasshopper's menu order: whether it needs an EPW and an analysis period, its score kind (weighted_sum or violation_count), its weight unit, the mode-specific settings it reads, its description and its starting values (what differs from the schema defaults: analysis period, tilted-plane angle, carve fraction). Also MODE_ALIASES and canonical_mode_name(). Validation, the CLI schema command, the stages and the Grasshopper components read their mode facts from here. Standard library only. archetype_defaults.py The shoebox archetype defaults (ARCHETYPE_DEFAULTS, WINDOW_TO_WALL_DEFAULTS, ARCHETYPE_OPTIONAL_KEYS) read by usc archetype, simulated_weights.py and the USC_Archetype component. Standard library only. errors.py UrbanSolarCarverError and its subclasses ConfigError (with ConfigFieldError), InputError, StageChainError, MalformedEngineRequest and RunCancelled, plus UrbanSolarCarverWarning. Standard library only. run_context.py RunContext (issues, progress callback, cancel flag), Issue, report_issue(), report_progress() and run_context() / stage_context(). Standard library only. stage_settings.py The per-stage settings models (PreprocessingSettings, ThresholdingSettings, ExportingSettings, MassingSettings, RunOptions), stages_to_rerun() and stage_folder() (the one definition of the <run_folder>/<stage> layout). Does not import torch. load_config.py Reads a YAML configuration file and returns a validated UserConfig object. load_config: loads the YAML, expands an analysis_period: mapping, resolves relative paths against the YAML's folder, applies flat key=value overrides, and validates with Pydantic (all errors reported in one message). build_config: validates typed values (what a client holds) into a UserConfig and raises ConfigError with a ConfigFieldError per problem; load_config calls it. parse_override_value: converts override strings into Python values (booleans, None, JSON lists and objects, numbers). chain_config.py The criteria: form of a config. load_chain validates a chain file into a ChainConfig: one Criterion (id, name, validated config) per criterion, built from the shared top-level settings plus the criterion's own. CRITERION_KEYS lists the per-criterion settings; every other key is shared. is_chain_file tells a chain file from an ordinary config; load_config refuses a chain file. See Criteria. pydantic_schemas.py Data schemas. UserConfig: the Pydantic v2 model defining every pipeline parameter with types, defaults and value ranges (e.g. voxel_size must be 0.01-100); unknown keys are rejected. It normalizes threshold into a ThresholdSpec, checks mode requirements, and emits UrbanSolarCarverWarning for settings the mode ignores and when ray_batch_size is clamped. PreprocessingManifest / ThresholdingManifest: schemas for the JSON manifests written by the first two stages, so a later stage can be re-run from an earlier run's output.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text: File Purpose compute_device.py The one rule for choosing the compute device. resolve_compute_device: auto/None picks CUDA when available, else the CPU; cpu, cuda, cuda:N and a torch.device are taken as given, and a CUDA choice without CUDA raises. warp_device_name: the Warp name of a torch device. Used by the stages, the session, the daemon, the weights, voxelization and the kernel launches. session.py Compute-session lifecycle. CarverSession: a long-lived object that keeps the CUDA context alive across pipeline calls and holds a value cache (voxelized grids, Tregenza patch directions and solid angles, and the sky-patch weights of the weighted modes). Keys cover the geometry, settings and device, so entries stay valid across runs; the cache holds at most 1 GiB (max_cache_bytes) and drops the least recently used entries beyond that. The daemon opens one session and keeps its cache between commands, returning only unused GPU memory after each; the Python API and CLI run without a session unless you open one (with CarverSession():). Compiled Warp kernels are cached by Warp itself, on disk. get_active_session: returns the session registered for a device, or None. session_cache: a decorator that stores a function's return value in the active session's cache under a key built from its arguments. engine_requests.py The request core every transport uses. parse_engine_request validates a message into a typed request (run, the stage commands, run_pipeline, simulate_weights, check, ping); config_for_engine_request builds its config from a YAML path or from the mode's starting values plus overrides. The check request runs one Simulate study (see Engine requests). A run request also carries trace_criteria and threshold_from_criterion (chain files) and after (one criterion, started at thresholding), and the ping reply lists the engine's features (run_after). handle_engine_request runs it in a run context and returns a typed reply with the run's issues; answer_engine_message does all of this for dict transports and turns any failure into an error reply with error_type and, for config errors, config_errors. Does not import torch until a request runs. daemon.py Persistent background process for Grasshopper and the CLI's --daemon flag, a transport over engine_requests. serve: listens on 127.0.0.1 (localhost only) with Python's multiprocessing.connection, authenticated with a random key stored in ~/.urbansolarcarver/.daemon_authkey. Creates a CarverSession on startup and keeps it for the daemon's lifetime; each request goes to answer_engine_message, and only shutdown is handled by the daemon itself. Started and stopped with the CLI (urbansolarcarver daemon start/stop) or from Grasshopper with the USC_Session component. daemon_client.py The client side of the daemon, standard library only: the authkey file (resolve_daemon_authkey), the default host and port, and send_daemon_request. The CLI's daemon commands use it, so they do not load torch; the daemon reads its key through it too. carver_cli.py Command-line interface built with Typer, registered in pyproject.toml as both urbansolarcarver and usc. Commands: run (the sequencer, with --produce and --start-from; it runs a chain file's criteria in order), preprocessing, thresholding (with --after for one step of a chain), exporting, massing (each with a config file -c, overrides -o, and optional --daemon), validate (lists a chain's criteria), schema (prints the config parameter table, filterable by --mode or --search), warmup, simulate-weights, archetype, ui (the browser interface) and daemon start/stop/status.

docs.title: Browser UI
docs.text:
File Purpose local_web_service/server.py The FastAPI application behind usc ui. create_app builds it; SecurityMiddleware refuses a Host header that is not the service's address and an API call or WebSocket without the launch token. Routes for projects, input files, settings, criteria, modes, examples, stage status, run summaries, result files, downloads and run events (see the routes below); serves the built front-end. Does not import torch. local_web_service/api_models.py The Pydantic models of the requests and replies; the front-end's types are generated from them. ProjectJson holds the project's criteria (CriterionEntry), next_criterion_id and the stage records, with the records of each criterion's preprocessing and thresholding in criterion_records. local_web_service/projects.py Project folders: name validation, the folder layout, project.json, uploads (several mesh files of a role are joined into one), the methods for criteria (add, update, delete, duplicate, reorder), config.yaml built from the settings the browser sends on top of the mode's starting values, and the voxel grid check. Every change that writes config.yaml checks it with load_chain first and writes nothing when the check fails. local_web_service/criteria.py The criterion model helpers: the colour palette, config.yaml generated from project.json (shared settings, then the criteria that are on), and the split of the app's settings into shared and criterion keys (split_settings). local_web_service/test_surfaces.py Test surface files stored once in inputs/test_surfaces/ and compared by content, the joined file of each criterion (inputs/joined/test_surfaces_<id>.ply) and of each study that lists files (inputs/joined/study_surfaces_<id>.ply), users_of (the criteria and studies that list a file; a stored file goes to the recycle bin when none does), and the fingerprint of a joined file that the stage records use. local_web_service/stored_files.py Input files replaced in the project folder from outside the app: the record of each stored file in project.json (stored_files: size, modification time, sha256), refresh_changed_inputs (a changed file builds again the joined files that use it; a joined file that comes out different replaces the old one, dates what was built on it and leaves a notice in changed_files), input_changes for the stage status, and the refusal of a run while a recorded file is missing. local_web_service/studies.py The studies of the Simulate workspace (StudyEntry, kept in project.json under studies beside the criteria): default names ("Sun hours, 21 Dec"), the settings a metric starts with and accepts (STUDY_SETTING_KEYS), a study like a criterion, and the results folder simulate/<id>. The store methods (add_study, update_study, delete_study, reorder_studies, use_study_test_surface, remove_study_test_surface) write project.json and the study's joined test surface file only, never config.yaml, inputs_revision or a stage record. local_web_service/simulation.py Running the studies: a study's check settings (north, ray length and carving spacing from the shared settings, rays per patch of the first criterion that is on, the study's metric, period, time basis and mode settings), its check engine request, why it cannot run (refusal_of), the engine's refusal of a study kept in simulate/<id>/refusal.json until its inputs change, its state (study_state: current, out of date when a file, setting or surface tolerance it was computed from changed, not run, refused) and the binary of its patches and values for the 3D view. Reads the result files through check_files.py, so it does not import torch. local_web_service/inspection.py The Inspect workspace's view of the input mesh files. inspect_file reads a stored file with load_mesh (the maximum volume and test surfaces with fix_normals) and keeps the result until its size or modification time changes; a surface is the triangles joined by shared edges, and a test surface file closed as a whole is not flippable. project_inspection: the summary of each mesh file (triangles, area, bounds, closed bodies, surfaces), a file that cannot be read listed with its problem. inspection_geometry: the triangles of a test surface file with a surface number per triangle, as one binary. save_turned_surfaces: turns whole surfaces, writes the file in its own format (OBJ at 10 decimals, PLY float64, GLB and STL float32), reads it back with load_mesh, saves nothing when the turns or corners did not hold, keeps the original in inputs/originals/test_surfaces/ before the first save and builds the joined files of the criteria and studies that list the file as an upload does. restore_original puts the kept original back. local_web_service/migration.py migrate_to_criteria: a project of an earlier version becomes a chain of one criterion with its results kept (run folders moved to run/criteria/1/, manifests that name them rewritten, records moved). It runs when a project opens, when a run starts and at a first settings save, and undoes its steps when one fails. local_web_service/stage_records.py Which stages of a project are current, out of date or missing, for each criterion (criterion_status) and summed up (stage_status), and which stages a run has to execute: choose_stages returns the criteria to trace (trace_criteria), the criterion to threshold from and what the run does for each criterion. local_web_service/run_worker.py Runs a project in a background thread in two phases (analysis, then envelope and massing), publishes progress events that name their criterion, refuses a run without test surfaces in a criterion that is on, and handles cancel. Runs a simulation of the studies (start_simulation, stage simulate) as the same kind of job: one job at a time, the same events and cancel, no stage record touched. local_web_service/run_summary.py, score_points.py What the app shows of a run: the numbers of the carving and massing for each criterion and for the chain, the sun path and sky dome, the scored voxels of a criterion, and which criterion carved each voxel. local_web_service/carve_further.py Carve further for a project with one criterion; refused with several. The browser app no longer offers it; the route stays for other clients. local_web_service/gpu_warm_up.py Compiles the GPU kernels in the background at launch and reports the device or why the CPU is used. example_projects/ The three packaged examples (examples.json, mesh files and one weather file). ui_static/ The built front-end, committed. build_info.json holds a hash of the sources in app/.

Routes for studies (Simulate; all under /api; the writes hold the project's lock and answer 409 while a run of the project is active; an unknown study id is a 404 that names the id):

Route What it does GET /projects/{name}/studies The studies in order, each with its state (current, out_of_date, not_run, refused with its reason) and the geometries its last result has, and the metrics with their availability, unit and default settings POST /projects/{name}/studies Add a study; body metric (its default period, no files) or from_criterion (the criterion's metric, period, mode settings and file names). Neither or both is a 422. Returns the StudyEntry PATCH /projects/{name}/studies/{id} Change name, metric, values (the study's settings) or target (null removes it). A new metric resets the settings to its defaults and keeps the values both metrics have DELETE /projects/{name}/studies/{id} Delete a study (204), move its results folder to the recycle bin and the stored test surface files no criterion or study lists PUT /projects/{name}/studies/order Reorder; body ids, every id once POST /projects/{name}/studies/{id}/test-surfaces Upload a test surface file to a study (multipart file) PUT /projects/{name}/studies/{id}/test-surfaces/{file} Use a file the project stores DELETE /projects/{name}/studies/{id}/test-surfaces/{file} Remove a file from a study POST /projects/{name}/simulate Run every study that can run as one job of the run worker (stage simulate, outside the pipeline's stages); events are read as a run's. 409 while any run or simulation is active, 422 when no study can run (the message names each study and why) GET /projects/{name}/studies/{id}/values The test point patches of the last result and the values of each geometry as one binary (layout in simulation.study_values); 404 without a result

None of these changes inputs_revision, config.yaml or a stage record.

Routes for Inspect (all under /api; the two writes hold the project's lock and answer 409 while a run of the project is active):

Route What it does GET /projects/{name}/inspect The InspectReply: the summary of each mesh file by role, allowed while a run is active GET /projects/{name}/inspect/test_surfaces/{file}/geometry The triangles of a test surface file with a surface number per triangle, as one binary (layout in inspection.inspection_geometry) POST /projects/{name}/inspect/test_surfaces/{file}/turn Body surfaces: turn those surfaces and save the file. 422 for a file closed as a whole, an unreadable file or a surface that does not exist, 500 when the written file does not read as turned (nothing is saved) POST /projects/{name}/inspect/test_surfaces/{file}/restore Put the kept original back; 404 when none is kept

Routes for criteria (all under /api; the writes hold the project's lock and answer 409 while a run of the project is active; an unknown criterion id is a 404 that names the id):

Route What it does GET /criterion-keys The settings that belong to a criterion (CRITERION_KEYS); every other setting is shared POST /projects/{name}/criteria Add a criterion at the end; body mode and optional name. Returns the CriterionEntry PATCH /projects/{name}/criteria/{id} Change name, colour, bypassed or values (the criterion's own settings; shared keys in values are ignored and belong to PUT /projects/{name}/shared-settings) DELETE /projects/{name}/criteria/{id} Delete a criterion (204) and the stored test surface files no other criterion uses POST /projects/{name}/criteria/{id}/duplicate Copy the settings and the test surface files into a new criterion at the end PUT /projects/{name}/criteria/order Reorder; body ids, every id once. A bad list is a 422 and changes nothing POST /projects/{name}/criteria/{id}/test-surfaces Upload a test surface file to a criterion (multipart file) PUT /projects/{name}/criteria/{id}/test-surfaces/{file} Use a stored file of another criterion DELETE /projects/{name}/criteria/{id}/test-surfaces/{file} Remove a file from a criterion GET /projects/{name}, PUT /projects/{name}/config Take an optional criterion (default: the first for a read, the only one for a save; a save with several criteria and none named is a 422). ProjectDetail gains criteria and criterion_status PUT /projects/{name}/shared-settings Save the settings the criteria share (body values, no mode); a criterion's own key is a 422 that names it, and so is a value that makes a criterion that is on invalid. Returns the shared settings as stored and the grid_plan GET /projects/{name}/criteria/{id}/settings The settings of one criterion with the shared ones (criterion_id, settings), read without looking at the test surface files GET /projects/{name}/sun-path Takes an optional criterion (default: the first criterion that is on) GET /projects/{name}/run/score-points, .../run/sky-patches Take an optional criterion (default: the last criterion that is on) GET /projects/{name}/run/carved-by-criterion One byte per voxel: the criterion that removed it (format in Browser UI)

POST /projects/{name}/runs answers with criterion_stages besides stages, and refuses with a 422 (missing_inputs) when no criterion is on or a criterion that is on has no test surfaces.

app/ holds the front-end source (src/inspect/ the Inspect workspace: InspectView.tsx, what it puts over the 3D view, FilesPanel.tsx, the Files panel with a file's summary, Flip mode, Save, Discard and Restore original, use_inspection.ts, the summaries, the selected file and the staged turns, UnsavedTurnsDialog.tsx, the Save, Discard or Stay question when leaving Inspect, and inspect_geometry_decoder.ts, the reader of the geometry binary; src/simulate/ the Simulate workspace: SimulateView.tsx, what it puts over the 3D view, StudiesPanel.tsx and AddStudyMenu.tsx, the Studies panel and its Add study menu, StudyPopover.tsx, a study's settings, GeometrySwitch.tsx and ResultCard.tsx, the geometry switch with Change and the result card, use_studies.ts and use_study_view.ts, the studies and the study on the view (geometry, Change, target, legend, card), and study_values.ts with study_values_decoder.ts, the statistics and the reader of the values binary; src/viewer_overlays/TargetLegend.tsx is its legend with the draggable target; src/steps/ the five steps: InputsStep.tsx, SiteAndGridStep.tsx, the result steps and the export, with ActionMenu.tsx, the menu of a project and of a criterion row, menu_popup.ts, the placement and keys of a popup menu that ActionMenu.tsx and the mode menu share, and CriteriaRunBar.tsx, the Run analysis and Build buttons pinned under the Criteria step; src/criteria/ the criteria hook and its helpers (use_criteria.ts, criteria_state.ts), the Criteria step, the criterion list and its rows (CriterionList.tsx, CriterionCard.tsx) and their dialogs, ModeMenu.tsx, the short menu of modes behind Add criterion, the criterion panel with PanelSection.tsx, its folded sections, and section_summaries.ts, the one-line summary of each section, and its Test surfaces box; src/settings_form/ the settings, with two_forms.ts for the shared and the criterion settings held side by side; src/viewer/ and src/viewer_overlays/ the 3D view, with carved_by_criterion_decoder.ts for the carved-by-criterion layer; src/api_client/ the typed client). See Browser UI for building it.

docs.title: Simulate
docs.text:
A carving protects sun, sky or solar energy on test surfaces. Simulate shows how much of it reaches each test point once the maximum volume stands (before) and once the carved envelope or the building massing stands (after), so you can see whether the carving did what it should. It is a quick check while designing, inside the browser UI. It traces triangle meshes, not voxels, and it does not replace a check of the finished design with an external tool.

Simulate is a workspace beside the pipeline. It changes no criterion, no shared setting and no pipeline step, and it starts nothing by itself: a study runs only when you press Run.

docs.title: Design and Simulate
docs.text:
The switch Design | Simulate in the header, next to the project name, changes the workspace. Simulate hides the steps and gives the 3D view the whole window. Design shows the step you left, with its folds and scroll position. The Layers menu and the viewer tools are the same in both. The context and the terrain are drawn in Simulate; the test surfaces of criteria and of other studies are not, only those of the selected study.

The Sky dome layer (Layers menu, off at first) is the selected study's, not Design's: each of the 145 sky patches coloured by the value it carried in the study's last run, the solar energy of the period from that patch for Solar energy and Useful solar gains (kWh/m²), its weight of the overcast sky, the night sky cooling or the sky for the three sky metrics. It changes with the study selected and is dimmed with it when the study is out of date. A sun hours study traces sun positions, not patches, so it has no dome; nor has a result run before the patch values were kept: the Layers menu then lists the Sky dome without a check box and says to run the study again.

docs.title: Studies
docs.text:
A study is a metric on test surface files over a period. The Studies panel floats over the top left of the 3D view and collapses to an icon. Each row has a colour swatch, the study's name and one line: its test surface files while its result is current, otherwise Out of date, Not run yet or the reason it cannot run (for example Add test surfaces). Pressing a row selects the study for the view: one study is on the view at a time, and its test surfaces are the ones coloured. When none is selected, the first study with a result is (or the first study), so a finished run shows its values without a press. The settings button of a row opens its popover.

Add study offers two kinds of entries in one menu:

  • Like criterion name makes a study from a criterion: the metric of its mode (see the table below), its period, the mode settings the metric reads and a copy of its test surface files. No link to the criterion is kept; changing the criterion later does not change the study.
  • A metric makes a study with the metric's default period and no test surface files. A metric that needs the weather file is greyed until the project has one.

The popover of a study holds:

Control Meaning Name A study is named from its metric and period, for example "Sun hours, 21 Dec" or "Useful solar gains, 15 Oct to 15 Apr". Typing a name keeps it from then on Metric One of the metrics below. Changing it resets the settings to those of the new metric and keeps the values both metrics have Analysis period The same control as in the Criteria step. Shown for the metrics that sum over a period More settings The few settings the metric reads: balance temperature, dead band and harm for useful solar gains; dew point and Bliss coefficient for the cooling sky; the time basis (standard, daylight saving or solar time) for sun hours Test surfaces The files the study uses. You can add new files (button or drop) or use a file the project stores already, for example a criterion's. A stored file is kept while a criterion or a study lists it and goes to the recycle bin when none does Delete study Removes the study and moves its results to the recycle bin. Its number is not used again

Every change is saved at once. The studies are stored in project.json under studies, apart from the criteria. They cannot be changed while a Design run or a simulation is going.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Each carving mode has a metric of the same quantity, which "Like criterion" takes. Any metric whose inputs exist can be chosen for a study.

Metric Unit Carving mode it matches Weather file Sun hours h Solar time-based needed Solar energy kWh/m² Solar energy needed Useful solar gains kWh/m² Solar usefulness needed Overcast sky component % Daylight not needed Cooling sky % Night cooling not needed Sky view factor % Angle rule not needed
  • Sun hours: hours of direct sun in the period. Each hour counts the sun position of that hour, and a position counts 1 h when it is above 5° altitude and in front of the test surface (no cosine of incidence). The 5° is the same for every study: "Like criterion" does not copy the minimum altitude of a time-based criterion, so a study counts the sun above 5° whatever the criterion's minimum altitude. The time basis says which clock the hours are read in; it is a setting of sun hours only. A new study starts at 21 December, 10 to 14 h.
  • Solar energy and Useful solar gains: direct and diffuse energy that reaches the surface in the period, from the weather file's Perez sky and the cosine of incidence. Useful solar gains count only the hours that need heating (the gains that heat the building; it was called useful solar energy before), with the balance temperature, dead band and weights of Solar usefulness. Ground reflection is left out. A new study starts with the whole year (solar energy) or 15 October to 15 April, 7 to 19 h (useful solar gains).
  • Overcast sky component: light from a CIE overcast sky. On a vertical facade this is the vertical sky component, at most 39.6 %.
  • Cooling sky: the long-wave cooling potential toward the clear night sky that the surface sees, from the dew point and the Bliss coefficient.
  • Sky view factor: the cosine-weighted share of the view taken by the sky. An unobstructed horizontal surface has 100 %, an unobstructed wall 50 %.

The three sky metrics are a percentage of what an unobstructed horizontal surface receives. Study names, units and the per-study defaults are listed by GET /projects/{name}/studies.

docs.title: What Simulate fixes
docs.text:
These choices are not settings:

  • Sky: Tregenza's 145 patches. Each patch is traced with jittered sub-rays, as the carving traces them, at the project's rays per patch (the value of the first criterion that is on, 4 when the project has no criterion). One ray per patch would leave gaps of about 12° between the rays and show banding.
  • Sun: one position per hour.
  • Test points: sampled on the study's test surfaces at the carving's spacing (the grid step of the shared settings, else half the voxel size). A study with more than 2 million test points is refused, and the message gives the spacing that fits.
  • Blocking: the context and the terrain of the project block in every geometry.
  • North and ray length come from the shared settings.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
The geometry switch at the top centre of the view chooses what the values are shown on. While a study's settings are open it moves to the right of the popover, and on windows narrower than 1000 px it sits at the top right, with the popover under the studies panel:

Geometry What blocks Max volume The maximum volume mesh as you added it (not its voxels) Envelope The envelope mesh that Build envelope wrote, clipped by the maximum volume Massing The building massing mesh, clipped by the maximum volume

The context and the terrain block in all three. With several criteria the envelope is the result of the whole chain. Envelope and Massing wait, with the reason as a tooltip, until Design has built them, and also when the selected study ran before they were built (the tooltip says to run the study again). A geometry that Design shows out of date is marked; Simulate still traces the mesh on disk.

Change colours each test point by its change from the maximum volume (the baseline) on the geometry shown: gains in Viridis from no change (dark) to the largest gain (yellow), losses in the colour the carving uses for carved voxels, a change smaller than a thousandth of the highest value without any geometry as none. Change waits while Max volume is shown.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Run runs every study that can run, for every geometry that is built: the maximum volume always, the envelope and the massing when they exist. Switching the geometry afterwards needs no new run. A study that cannot run says why on its row (no test surface files, no maximum volume, no weather file for a metric that needs one, a setting the engine refuses). One that the engine refuses, for example for too many test points, keeps its message until its inputs change, and the other studies still run.

There is one job at a time. While a Design run is going, Run shows "A Design run is in progress" and waits; while a simulation is going, Design's run buttons say so. Nothing is queued. The progress shows under Run with a Cancel button.

docs.title: The legend, the colour range and the result card
docs.text:
The legend along the bottom of the view shows the scale the values are coloured by, with a switch between two:

  • Value in the study's unit (for example kWh/m²), the default: each point coloured by its value.
  • % of no-build: each point coloured by its share of its no-build value, its value with nothing built on the plot (no maximum volume, envelope or massing). The surroundings and the terrain still block, so the no-build value is not a value without any context: it is the most each point can receive in the city as it is. The scale runs from 0 to 100 %, the same for every geometry, so Max volume, Envelope and Massing compare directly. A point that gets nothing in the no-build case (a facade that sees no sun in the period, say) loses nothing, so it counts as 100 %.

A study's values spread mostly with the way each surface faces: on Allatini's Solar energy study the roofs reach about 1,550 kWh/m² while the facades lie between 200 and 800. By value, move the high end down to the facades' range to see their differences (below); by share, every point is measured against its own no-build value, and the maximum volume keeps 78 % of the no-build value there and the envelope 99 %.

The colour range. Two marks on the legend set the low and the high end of the colours. The palette runs between them, and a value beyond an end takes that end's colour, so the colours can spread over the values that matter (the facades between 200 and 800 kWh/m², say, rather than 0 to the roofs' 1,550). Drag a mark, or press on the bar to move the nearer one; or focus a mark and use the arrow keys (1 % of the bar), Page Up and Page Down (10 %) and Home and End; Delete puts it back to its default. The ends cannot pass each other. By value the low end is the study's target and the high end its upper end, both saved with the study (by default 0 and the highest value of the geometry shown); the result card's "at target" counts the points at or above the low end. By share the ends are percentages, 0 and 100 by default, kept for each study while the app is open.

The palettes are fixed: Magma by value, Viridis by share and for Change. Both are matplotlib's perceptually even palettes, from dark to light without a grey middle (Viridis is the one most readable with the common colour vision deficiencies), so the two colourings do not look alike. In the Change view the legend shows the change ramp instead, without ends, and the loss colour when some point lost.

The result card in the bottom right corner is for the selected study on the geometry shown. It gives:

  • what the geometry keeps of the no-build value: the sum of its values over the sum with nothing built on the plot, for example "keeps 99 % of the no-build value (78)",
  • the mean,
  • the lowest tenth (10th percentile),
  • with a target (the low end by value), the share of points at or above it.

On Envelope and Massing each line has the maximum volume's value in brackets, for example "mean 3.6 h (4.1)".

docs.title: Out of date
docs.text: A result is out of date when any of these changed since it was computed: the study's settings (including its metric and period), its test surface files, the weather file, the context, the terrain, the maximum volume, or the envelope or massing mesh it traced (including one built or removed). The surface tolerance of the envelope and massing, which follows the voxel size they were built with, counts too. So do the shared settings a study reads: north, the ray length, the test point spacing (the voxel size and the grid step) and the rays per patch of the first criterion that is on. Turning a criterion on or off in Design can therefore make every study out of date. The result stays on the view, dimmed, with the Out of date stamp at the top of the view, and the row says "Out of date". Nothing reruns by itself: press Run. Moving the project folder does not make a result out of date. Changing the target does not either. A file saved over an input file in the project folder counts as a change once the app has found it (see Replacing a file in the project folder).

docs.title: Where the results are kept
docs.text:
Each study's results are in <project>/simulate/<study number>/:

File Content check_points.npz The test points, their normals, the corners of the square patch each draws and the frame the coordinates are relative to check_values.npz One value per point for each geometry (open with no geometry, max_volume, then envelope and massing when traced) check_sky.json The value of each of the 145 sky patches for the study's metric, drawn as the study's sky dome; none for sun hours check_summary.json The metric, unit, settings, and for each geometry its mesh, triangle count, surface tolerance and statistics, and what the result was computed from. It is written last, so a folder without it has no result refusal.json Only for a study the engine refused: the message and the inputs it was refused with

Reopening the project shows the last results. The studies also use inputs/joined/study_surfaces_<number>.ply, the joined test surface file of a study, beside the criteria's.

The service routes are under /projects/{name}/studies and POST /projects/{name}/simulate; the engine request is check (see Engine requests).

docs.title: The Sun panel
docs.text:
The Sun panel, under the studies panel and collapsed at first (the sun icon opens it), shows the site with the sun as architects study it on a sun path diagram and with shadow drawings, beside the studies. Opening it shows the sun on the view; collapsing it takes everything of the sun away again. It needs the project's weather file, whose location gives the sun's course; without one it says so. North is the project's, as in the carving.

  • The sun path is drawn while the panel is open, on the hemisphere around the scene: the sun's arcs on the March equinox (the September one lies within a fraction of a degree of it) and the two solstices (dashed), a line for each whole hour showing where the sun stands at that hour through the year (labelled at its highest point), the day's arc (bold) and, at a moment, the sun.
  • A switch chooses what the view shows besides the sun path, one at a time: Sun path only, Shadows at a time or Hours in shade. Each has its own controls.
  • Clock, at the end: the times are read as the weather file's local standard time, local solar time (noon when the sun crosses the meridian) or local daylight saving time (an hour ahead of standard time on every date, as the engine reads it).

Shadows at a time is a moment: a day on a year strip (with 21 Mar, 21 Jun, 21 Sep and 21 Dec as presets) and a time on a day strip, each with one handle, as the criteria panel's strips are drawn (drag the handle or press on the strip; the arrow keys move a day or 5 minutes, Page Up and Page Down a month or an hour). The panel says how high the sun stands and its bearing from north, or that it is below the horizon. The scene is lit by the sun at that moment: the maximum volume, the envelope, the massing, the surroundings and the terrain cast shadows on each other, and on the ground where there is no terrain. The sky light is lowered meanwhile, so the shade reads.

Hours in shade is a period: the criteria panel's analysis period control, a range of days on the year strip and a range of hours on the day strip (the end hour counted: 8 to 15 h is 08:00 to 16:00; days across the new year and hours across midnight wrap), with its presets. For every surface the view shows it counts how many of those hours the surface spends in shade, on the one day or as a mean per day over the days. A surface is in shade at a time when something stands between it and the sun or it faces away from the sun. Colours chooses viridis (yellow in sun all the range, dark in shade all of it) or grey (light to dark). The colours are drawn under the sun path and the compass ring, which stay visible over them.

The hours in shade are a quick count, not a study. They are worked out on the graphics card from the camera: the view is drawn once for each sun position (every 10 minutes on one day, every 30 minutes over several days, on every n-th day when that would be more than 240 positions), and each draw adds the time it stands for where the surface is in shade. So the count is of what the camera sees, at the resolution of the shadow map (4096 pixels across about five times the site's radius), and it is counted again when the camera stops moving. A Sun hours study is the precise count, per test point, traced against the meshes.

The Show switch beside the studies panel's title hides the selected study from the view (its colours, legend and result card) and shows it again, for a clear view of the shadows or the hours in shade.

The panel reads two routes: GET /projects/{name}/sun-chart?date=MM-DD&time_basis= (the arcs of the March equinox, the solstices and date, every 5 minutes, and an hour line for each whole hour, a point a week) and GET /projects/{name}/sun-positions?from=MM-DD&to=MM-DD&start=&end=&step=&time_basis= (the sun above the horizon every step minutes from minute start to end of each day from from to to, over the new year when to comes first and over midnight when end comes before start, with its altitude and azimuth; on every n-th day, day_step, when that would be more than 240 positions). time_basis is standard (the default), solar or daylight_saving. Both answer 404 without a weather file.

docs.title: Not there yet
docs.text:
These belong to a later milestone:

  • studies on other designs (meshes added for Simulate only),
  • snapshots of results,
  • CSV export of the values,
  • side-by-side views with linked cameras,
  • a command-line command and a Grasshopper component for the check.

docs.title: Simulated Benefit Weights
docs.text: Benefit mode's optional simulated weighting runs a small building simulation inside USC. A simulation brings physical assumptions that the geometric parts of USC do not have, so this page documents the engine, its origin, how it was validated, what the user supplies, and where its limits are.

docs.title: The engine
docs.text:
USC implements the ISO 13790 Annex C simple hourly method, commonly called the 5R1C model: a single thermal zone represented by five conductances and one lumped thermal-mass capacitance.

  • Nodes: outdoor air, supply air, indoor air, an internal surface node, and the thermal mass.
  • Conductances: ventilation, air-surface coupling, glazing, surface-mass coupling, and the opaque-envelope remainder, all derived per the standard (coupling coefficients h_is = 3.45 W/m²K, h_ms = 9.1 W/m²K, Λ_at = 4.5; thermal mass per ISO 13790 Table 12 mass classes).
  • Time stepping: Crank-Nicolson on the mass node, one hour per step, with the standard's three-step heating/cooling demand calculation (free-float, 10 W/m² test load, exact linear interpolation to the setpoint).

On top of the simulation sits perturbation attribution: for every hour of the year, the transmitted solar gain of that hour is perturbed by ±1 W and the change in annual heating and cooling demand is attributed to that hour (central differences). This yields two hourly series in [0, 1]:

Series Meaning benefit[t] fraction of a marginal joule of solar gain at hour t that offsets heating over the year harm[t] fraction that becomes cooling load

Attributing against the annual totals captures thermal lag: a noon gain stored in the mass and released into the cold evening still earns heating credit. All 17,521 year-simulations (the base run plus two per hour) run as one vectorized NumPy batch, in seconds.

docs.title: Origin and validation
docs.text:
The engine is an independent implementation, written directly from the ISO 13790 Annex C equation set in NumPy (urbansolarcarver/simulated_weights.py). It is not a fork, port, or adaptation of an existing simulator.

It is cross-validated against RC_BuildingSimulator, the ETH Zurich Architecture & Building Systems group's MIT-licensed implementation of the same annex (Jayathissa et al., "Optimising building net energy demand with dynamic BIPV shading", Applied Energy 202, 2017). The validation setup:

  • Three archetype scenarios: medium office, heavy masonry, light insulated.
  • Weather: the bundled Golden, CO TMY3 EPW (dry-bulb direct; transmitted solar from Ladybug's directional irradiance on each scenario's glazing, g = 0.6).
  • Compared quantities: annual heating and cooling demand totals (agreement to roughly 1 Wh/year, relative tolerance 1e-6), mean annual air temperature, and hourly air-temperature, mass-temperature, and heating/cooling-demand values at sampled hours across the year.
  • Method: the oracle's own derived conductances are fed into USC's engine directly, so the comparison isolates the hourly recurrence itself rather than parameter-derivation conventions (the two implementations intentionally differ on one of those: RC_BuildingSimulator uses U·A directly for the opaque-envelope conductance, USC applies the standard's serial split).
  • Artifacts: the oracle's driving arrays and reference outputs are committed verbatim in tests/data/oracle_5r1c_reference.json; the regression runs in the test suite on every change (tests/test_simulated_weights.py), deterministically, with no weather generation at test time.

Beyond the oracle comparison, the engine is checked for steady-state energy-balance closure against an independent hand-derived network reduction (constant outdoor temperature, no gains: demand converges to conductance × ΔT with the air node held at setpoint), and for the physical property that heavier mass classes flatten hour-to-hour mass-temperature variation.

Full derivation notes and the coefficient provenance live in the repository at design/simulated-weights.md.

docs.title: What you supply: the archetype
docs.text:
The archetype describes a typical building in about ten numbers. Two equivalent forms are accepted (configs/archetype_example.yaml shows both):

Shoebox form (areas derived for you):

Key Meaning width, length, height zone dimensions (m); floor area, volume, facade areas derived wwr window-to-wall ratio per facade, keyed north/east/south/west g_value glazing solar transmittance (applies to all windows) orientation optional rotation of the whole box, degrees clockwise from north

Explicit form: floor_area, volume, area_opaque, area_window, and a windows list of [azimuth_deg, area_m2, g_value].

Both forms additionally take: u_opaque, u_window (W/m²K), ach_vent, ach_infiltration (1/h), heat_recovery (0-1), mass_class (very_light … very_heavy, ISO 13790 Table 12), t_set_heating, t_set_cooling (°C), and internal gains as either a flat internal_gains_w_m2 (W/m², default 5) or a 24-value daily profile internal_gains_profile_w_m2.

Shading coefficients (optional, declared multipliers; no device geometry is modelled):

Key Meaning shading_permanent year-round solar transmission multiplier in [0, 1] (fins, context obstructions); 1 = no shading shading_hot additional multiplier applied only during hot_months (awnings, tents, seasonal vegetation); stacks with the permanent factor hot_months calendar months (1-12) when shading_hot is deployed, e.g. [6, 7, 8, 9]

Each coefficient accepts a scalar (all facades) or a per-facade mapping ({south: 0.8, west: 0.9}); windows are assigned to their nearest cardinal facade. The perturbation attribution is attenuated by the same factors, so the weights describe a marginal joule of exterior solar: a July joule arriving while the awning is out counts for little. The declared coefficients are recorded in the artifact's provenance. Note that a fixed overhang's blocking is concentrated in high-sun hours, so its effect is usually best expressed through shading_hot rather than shading_permanent.

The shipped example values are deliberately neutral, with no national defaults. For real projects, source values from TABULA (EU building-stock typologies), DOE prototype buildings (US), or your national code tables.

The usc archetype command builds and validates the file for you, printing the derived floor area, volume, and per-facade window areas so mistakes surface before any simulation runs:

usc archetype -o my_building.yaml -s width=12 -s wwr_south=0.4 -s mass_class=heavy
usc archetype --from my_building.yaml -o variant.yaml -s mass_class=light   # derive a variant

In Grasshopper, USC_Archetype assembles the archetype from five family feeder components (USC_ZoneGeometry / Fabric / Ventilation / Operation / Shading, one wire each), feeding USC_SimulateWeights, whose output path wires into USC_BenefitParams.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The weights are a marginal, single-zone, schedule-free physical signal. They capture effects the binary balance-point rule cannot (thermal lag, mass state, gain saturation), but the model makes the following simplifications on purpose:

  • Single zone, lumped mass: the weights are facade-independent within an hour; time-of-day carries the directional signal. Perimeter-zone effects are out of scope for a massing tool.
  • Ideal, unlimited conditioning at the air node; continuous operation, no setback or occupancy schedules.
  • Fixed air-change rates: no night flushing, and no adaptive shading control. Without a declared shading_hot coefficient the harm channel is overstated, since real buildings have cheap defenses against summer sun that they lack for missing winter sun; declaring seasonal shading in the archetype makes harm a defensible estimate instead of a worst case. include_harm remains opt-in.
  • Flat internal gains, or one 24-hour profile repeated every day.
  • Marginal linearization: the weights describe one extra watt at the archetype's operating point; window sizes and g-values in the archetype set where gains saturate, and are recorded in the artifact's provenance metadata.
  • Unshaded derivation: the weights are computed for an unshaded archetype while the carve itself creates shading context; a first-order acceptable inconsistency for massing studies.
  • TMY weather; the ISO coupling coefficients carry the standard's residential-European calibration provenance.

Treat include_harm as a bracketing scenario

Without declared seasonal shading, harm is conservatively overstated (no night ventilation is modelled either), so the benefit-only weighting is the recommended default. Declaring shading_hot + hot_months in the archetype makes the harm channel a defensible estimate; even then, enable the subtraction deliberately for overheating-critical projects rather than as the standard mode.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text: Every artifact records its full provenance (meta: method, EPW, the complete expanded archetype, perturbation size, timestamp), and every carve that consumes one records that provenance in its preprocessing diagnostics. The artifact file is read again on every preprocessing run, so a regenerated artifact takes effect on the next run. With diagnostic_plots: true, the run also writes a comparison dome quantifying how the simulated weights shifted the sky relative to the simple rule under the same configuration.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Carving Modes: benefit for the user-level workflow
  • Tutorial 5 (examples/5_benefit_5r1c.ipynb) for an end-to-end walkthrough
  • API reference for generate_simulated_weights(), ZoneParams, and the artifact I/O

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The Python suite (about 1330 tests in tests/) and the front-end suite (about 480 vitest tests in app/) run locally: there is no CI, because the engine runs on the GPU and hosted runners have none. Tests marked gpu are skipped automatically without CUDA.

Install the test dependencies once with pip install -e .[dev] (it includes pytest-xdist, which runs tests in parallel with -n). Run the commands below from the repository root with the repository's environment active. In a git worktree that has no environment of its own, put the worktree's sources first: PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest ... (in PowerShell, $env:PYTHONPATH = "src" once).

docs.title: Four tiers
docs.text:
Times are wall times on an 8-core / 16-thread AMD Zen 2 with an RTX 3060, measured 2026-10-19.

Tier When Command Time 0 While editing python -m pytest tests/test_floor_plates.py -m "not slow" seconds 1 After every change python -m pytest -m "not slow" -n 8 about 45 s 2 Before each commit python -m pytest -m "not sweep" -n 8 about 65 s 3 Before merging python -m pytest -n 8 about 100 s

When app/ changed, also run the front-end checks of the same tier (see below): npm test takes about 12 s, npm run typecheck 5 s and npm run build 7 s.

docs.title: Tier 0: the files you are editing
docs.text:
Run the test file of the module you are changing, or one test with -k:

python -m pytest tests/test_floor_plates.py -m "not slow"
python -m pytest tests/test_floor_plates.py -k end_wings

--lf runs only the tests that failed last time, which is quick after a fix. In app/:

npx vitest run src/steps/ModeStep.test.tsx

docs.title: Tier 1: after every change
docs.text:
python -m pytest -m "not slow" -n 8

Leaves out the tests marked slow: end-to-end scenes, full-year simulations, sweeps and a real daemon process. When app/ changed, in a second terminal at the same time:

cd app
npm test && npm run typecheck

docs.title: Tier 2: before each commit
docs.text:
python -m pytest -m "not sweep" -n 8

Everything except the tests marked sweep (the 0.5 m floor-plate sweep and the Monte Carlo seeds). When app/ changed, rebuild the front end first: the pytest run includes the test that compares ui_static/build_info.json with the sources.

cd app
npm test && npm run build

npm run build runs the type check before it writes src/urbansolarcarver/ui_static/.

docs.title: Tier 3: before merging
docs.text:
python -m pytest -n 8

The whole suite, sweeps included. From time to time, and before a release, run it without -n (about 5 minutes): a serial run catches a test that only passes after another one has run. Also run, when they apply:

  • after a change to the engine's numerics, the randomised Monte Carlo sweep: python tests/montecarlo.py (see its docstring for the options);
  • after a change under grasshopper/components/, the Rhino smoke test tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py (see Grasshopper);
  • before a release, the suite in a fresh install (see CONTRIBUTING.md, "Checking a fresh install").

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
Marker Meaning Left out by slow Takes seconds: end-to-end scenes, simulations, a daemon process -m "not slow" sweep Exhaustive parameter sweeps and Monte Carlo seeds; always also slow -m "not sweep" gpu Needs a CUDA GPU; skipped automatically without one (automatic)

Mark a new test slow when it takes more than about a second, and sweep when it repeats a check over many parameter values that other tests already cover at a few chosen ones. pyproject.toml runs pytest with --strict-markers (a misspelt marker is an error) and --durations=15 (every run ends with its 15 slowest tests). After the run, tests/conftest.py also lists each test outside slow that took over 1 s; mark it slow or make it faster. Times grow by about half under -n 8, so a test listed only in a parallel run may be fine on its own.

An exact count in a test (panels, sample points, kept voxels of a packaged example) carries a comment on how to take the new value after a deliberate change of the example files or of the code that produces it.

docs.title: Running in parallel
docs.text: -n 8 starts 8 worker processes and hands out single tests to them; each worker pays about 8 s of imports and collection once. Tests must not depend on one another or on a shared file: each uses its own tmp_path. The engine computes each sky matrix in a temporary folder of its own, so workers computing sky matrices at the same time do not share Ladybug's weather folder. When another checkout is testing on the same machine at the same time, -n 4 leaves it room.

docs.title: Browser UI
docs.text: usc ui opens UrbanSolarCarver in your browser. You add the maximum volume, add the test surfaces and choose a mode for a criterion (a project can carve with several criteria, one after the other), run the analysis, adjust how much to carve while watching the result in 3D, build the envelope and building massing, and download the files. It runs the same engine as the CLI and the Python API; everything stays on your computer.

docs.title: Starting the interface
docs.text:
In the UrbanSolarCarver folder, double-click start-urbansolarcarver.bat on Windows, or run ./start-urbansolarcarver.sh in a terminal on Linux and macOS. The first time, the launcher installs UrbanSolarCarver with setup_env.py (this takes several minutes and needs Python 3.10 or newer); after that it starts the interface at once. A window stays open while the interface runs: close it (Windows) or press Ctrl+C (Linux, macOS) to stop UrbanSolarCarver. The launcher passes its arguments on to usc ui, so start-urbansolarcarver.bat --port 8780 works too. It uses the environment in .venv in the folder, or ~/.usc-venv when setup_env.py had to put it there; for an environment made with setup_env.py --venv-dir, set USC_VENV to that folder.

From a terminal with the environment active, the same command is:

usc ui

The command prints the address to open and opens it in your default browser once the service is listening. When another program already uses the port, the command says so and stops without opening the browser; choose a free port with --port. The address carries a token that is new on every launch, so keep using the page it opened (or the printed address) and not a bookmark from an earlier launch. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop the service.

Option Default Meaning --port 8770 Port on 127.0.0.1 --projects-folder the folder chosen in the app, else ~/UrbanSolarCarver/projects Folder that holds one subfolder per project; it is created when missing. It wins over the folder chosen in the app for that launch --no-browser off Print the address without opening the browser --device, -d auto Compute device: auto, cpu or cuda

The browser interface is an optional extra of the package. setup_env.py installs it unless you pass --no-ui; to add it to an existing environment run python -m pip install -e ".[ui]" (see Installation). Without the extra, usc ui prints that command and exits, and every other command is unaffected.

When the service starts it compiles the GPU kernels in the background. The start screen shows "Preparing the GPU" until that ends; you can open a project and add files meanwhile, and the run buttons wait for the GPU.

docs.title: The start screen
docs.text:
The start screen shows the version, the device (the GPU's name, or that the CPU is used) and three cards:

  • New project: type a name (up to 64 letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens or underscores) and create the project.
  • Open a project: the projects folder, with Change folder, and the projects in it, newest first. Each project has a menu (see Managing a project).
  • Try an example: three projects with their files already in place, so you can run an analysis without preparing any input. Perimeter block (a perimeter block 126 by 92 m, mode Solar time-based) is the smallest, New building among neighbors (a plot of about 18 by 17 m among existing buildings, mode Solar energy) is the middle one, and District of many buildings (about 208 by 227 m, mode Solar energy) is the largest. The first time you choose an example, it makes a copy as a new project, so the example itself never changes. After that, choosing it opens that project again. A project records which example it came from, so it is found after a rename. To start from a fresh copy, use Reset to the example in the project's menu.

docs.title: The projects folder
docs.text:
Change folder opens the operating system's folder picker on this computer. The browser never sends a path: the service shows the picker and reads the folder you choose. The folder is remembered in ~/.urbansolarcarver/ui.json and used at the next launch. The projects already in the old folder stay there, and the list shows the projects of the new folder.

  • Change folder is offered on the start screen only, with no run active. While a run is active the start screen says the folder can be changed once the run has ended.
  • When the folder was given with --projects-folder, it wins for that launch and the start screen offers no Change folder. Start usc ui without the option to change it there.
  • When the folder picker cannot open (no display, or tkinter missing), the start screen says so and the old folder stays. The way that always works is to start with usc ui --projects-folder <folder>.

docs.title: Managing a project
docs.text:
Each project in the list, and the project name in the top bar, has a menu:

  • Open folder opens the project's folder in Explorer (Finder, or the file manager on Linux) on this computer. It works during a run.
  • Rename asks for a new name, checked by the same rule as a new project's name, and renames the folder.
  • Delete names the project and its folder and asks you to type the project name to confirm.
  • Reset to the example (projects made from an example) replaces the project's inputs, settings and results with a fresh copy of the example, after a confirmation. The project keeps its name.

Rename, delete and reset wait while the project's run is active.

Delete and Reset send the project folder to the recycle bin (Windows) or trash (macOS, Linux), so a mistake can be undone; UrbanSolarCarver does not delete it for good. They remove only that one project folder, and refuse when the folder is not a direct child of the projects folder, has no project.json of that project, or is or holds a symbolic link or junction. On Windows they work only for a folder on a fixed disk of this computer: on a network, removable or other drive they are refused, and you can delete the folder in the file manager. A folder larger than the recycle bin's size limit may be deleted for good by Windows, and the app cannot check this beforehand.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
A project opens as a list of five steps on the left, with the 3D view on the right. Each step shows a one-line summary when it is closed.

  1. Inputs. The site: drop or choose the maximum volume (the largest building you would allow) and, for the modes that need one, a weather file (.epw). The test surfaces belong to each criterion (step 3). Two boxes are optional: Existing surroundings (buildings and large trees that stay, context_path; not balconies or shading devices) and Terrain (the ground, terrain_path). Both block sun and sky; nothing is built in the columns the surroundings take, and the site stays buildable above the terrain (see Context and terrain). Removing their files makes the analysis out of date, and the next run goes without them. With either of them, Site and grid shows Account for context blocking (on by default; not in the Angle rule, which traces no rays to the sky): off, they still take their voxels but block no sun or sky, to compare the two carvings. Meshes may be PLY, OBJ, STL or GLB; several files for one role are joined into one. The step lists each file with its triangle count and the size of all inputs together, and warns when the model looks as if it is not in meters.
  2. Site and grid. The analysis settings every criterion shares, with plain labels, units and a help text for each: north, the surroundings switch and the detail (voxel size, then, folded, the rays per batch and the detailed statistics, which only change the run report). The sample spacing on the test surfaces, the grid margin and the ray length have no field: the engine's values apply (see below). The step shows the size of the voxel grid and refuses a grid larger than the analysis can handle, naming the smallest voxel size that fits. Run analysis is pinned under the steps while it is open. Its summary reads "North 10°, 0.5 m voxels". See Entering values.

  3. Criteria. A criterion is one carving pass with its own test surfaces, mode and carving rule. The step always shows the list of criteria, also with one criterion (a new project starts with one), then the panel of the selected criterion, and keeps Run analysis and Build envelope and massing pinned under the steps while it is open. In this order (the rows, Add criterion and the pinned bar are described under Several criteria):

    • The list: one row per criterion in carving order, each with a colour swatch, its name, the symbol of its mode, its result or state, a switch that is on and a menu. Add criterion, under the list, opens a short menu of the six modes.

    • The panel of the selected criterion, in four sections, each a button with the section's title and, while it is closed, a one-line summary of what it holds. Test surfaces and Carving rule start open, Mode and Settings closed; the sections you open or close stay as you left them when you select another criterion.

      • Test surfaces (summary: the file name, two file names, "3 files" or "None yet"): the criterion's test surfaces (the surfaces whose sun or sky the carving protects), a drop box like the Inputs boxes. While it has none, the box says Add test surfaces with a hint of what its mode may protect (Daylight: windows or facades; Solar energy: roofs or facades), and Run analysis waits for them.
      • Mode (summary: the mode's plain name): six tiles in a grid of three by two, each with a coloured symbol and a plain name. The tile's tooltip holds a one-line description, what the mode needs and the engine name, for people who use the CLI.
      Tile Engine name What it does Angle rule tilted_plane Removes everything above a plane at a fixed angle from each facade Solar time-based time-based Keeps direct sun on the test surfaces during the hours you choose Solar energy irradiance Keeps sun and sky energy over the period Solar usefulness benefit Keeps sun in the hours that need heating Daylight daylight Keeps the view of an overcast sky Night cooling radiative_cooling Keeps a flat roof's view of the cold night sky. Experimental, and it assumes horizontal test surfaces

      Choosing a mode fills its starting values in the Settings section. Carving Modes explains the methods. - Settings (summary: the analysis period in words, "21 Dec, 7 to 19 h", in the modes that have one; otherwise "Starting values" or "2 settings changed"): the analysis period, the mode's own settings and, folded, the rays per sky patch in the four sky-patch modes. - Carving rule (summary: "Carve 70 %", "Cutoff 1.5 m²·h", "Automatic", or "Everything above the planes" in the Angle rule): how much to carve, with a histogram of the scores of the voxels (a log or linear scale) and the numbers of the last carving.
